questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man presents with a 10-year history of left ear discharge described as foul-smelling and non-pulsatile. He now reports progressive left-sided hearing loss and new-onset facial weakness (House-Brackmann Grade III). Otoscopy reveals a retraction pocket in the posterosuperior quadrant of the pars tensa with white debris and granulation tissue. CT temporal bone shows erosion of the scutum and lateral wall of the epitympanum. What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.A: Systemic antibiotics and ear toilet for 6 weeks followed by reassessment
options.B: Modified radical mastoidectomy with facial nerve decompression
options.C: Cortical mastoidectomy alone
options.D: High-resolution MRI of the internal auditory canal to rule out acoustic neuroma

questions.explanation: This is a classic presentation of acquired cholesteatoma with intratemporal complication (facial nerve palsy). Key features: foul-smelling discharge (keratin debris infection), retraction pocket in posterosuperior quadrant (attic/sinus cholesteatoma), scutum erosion on CT, and new facial weakness (House-Brackmann III). The presence of facial nerve involvement mandates surgical intervention — modified radical mastoidectomy (exteriorization technique) along with facial nerve decompression is the procedure of choice when cholesteatoma has eroded into the fallopian canal. Option A (antibiotics) is inappropriate with established intratemporal complication and structural erosion. Option C (cortical mastoidectomy alone) is used for acute mastoiditis without cholesteatoma; it does not address the epithelial disease or facial nerve. Option D (MRI IAC) is irrelevant here — the clinical picture points to cholesteatoma, not a retrocochlear lesion. High-yield pearl: In cholesteatoma, facial palsy is usually due to erosion of the tympanic segment of the facial nerve (most common site of injury in cholesteatoma). House-Brackmann III = moderate dysfunction; surgery should not be delayed. Exam trap: Do not confuse with benign paroxysmal positional vertigo or Meniere's disease — foul discharge + scutum erosion + facial palsy = cholesteatoma until proven otherwise.

questions.question_text: A 6-year-old child is brought with complaints of bilateral decreased hearing for 3 months, poor performance in school, and occasional ear pain. He had recurrent episodes of acute otitis media in the past year. Examination reveals the tympanic membrane findings shown in the image above. Pure tone audiometry shows bilateral flat conductive hearing loss of 35 dB. Tympanometry shows a Type B flat curve bilaterally. What is the MOST appropriate first-line management?

options.A: Bilateral myringotomy with ventilation tube (grommet) insertion
options.B: Watchful waiting for 3 months with hearing reassessment
options.C: Adenoidectomy alone
options.D: Systemic corticosteroids for 2 weeks

questions.explanation: This child has Otitis Media with Effusion (OME / 'glue ear') with bilateral conductive hearing loss of 35 dB persisting for 3 months, Type B tympanogram, and documented school impact. The image shows classic OME features: amber discolouration, fluid level, absent light reflex, no perforation. Per international guidelines (SIGN, AAO-HNS), watchful waiting is appropriate for <3 months of OME without hearing loss >25 dB. However, this child already has: (1) hearing loss ≥35 dB, (2) documented duration ≥3 months, (3) speech/educational impact. These are indications for grommet insertion. Grommet insertion is the single most effective intervention for bilateral OME with significant hearing loss. Option B is incorrect here because the child already meets intervention criteria. Option C (adenoidectomy alone) may reduce recurrence but does not immediately restore hearing; it is often performed alongside grommet insertion, not alone. Option D (corticosteroids) show short-term benefit but no long-term effect and are not first-line per current guidelines. High-yield pearl: Type B tympanogram = flat, no peak = middle ear effusion. Type A = normal. Type C = negative middle ear pressure. Exam trap: Many candidates confuse 'watchful waiting' threshold — it applies only when OME is <3 months AND hearing loss is <25 dB AND no developmental impact.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden onset left-sided sensorineural hearing loss that developed overnight. She denies trauma, noise exposure, or otorrhea. She had a mild upper respiratory tract infection 2 weeks ago. On examination, the tympanic membrane is normal. Pure tone audiometry shows left sensorineural hearing loss of 65 dB across all frequencies with poor speech discrimination. MRI of the internal auditory canal is normal. What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.A: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day for 10–14 days
options.B: Intravenous acyclovir for herpes simplex encephalitis
options.C: Immediate cochlear implant evaluation
options.D: Intratympanic gentamicin injection

questions.explanation: This is Sudden Sensorineural Hearing Loss (SSNHL) — defined as ≥30 dB loss across ≥3 consecutive frequencies occurring within 72 hours. The etiology is unknown in most cases (idiopathic SSNHL), but viral, vascular, and autoimmune causes are proposed. The preceding URI suggests viral aetiology. Normal MRI rules out vestibular schwannoma. Treatment of choice: Oral systemic corticosteroids (prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day, max 60 mg, for 10–14 days with taper) — the only evidence-based first-line therapy per AAO-HNS 2019 guidelines. Option B (acyclovir): Antivirals are NOT recommended as monotherapy or as adjunct to steroids per current guidelines (level A evidence against). Option C (cochlear implant): Premature — cochlear implant is considered only after failure of medical therapy and in patients with bilateral profound SSNHL. Option D (intratympanic gentamicin): This is used for Meniere's disease to ablate vestibular function — completely wrong here and would worsen hearing loss. Intratympanic dexamethasone (not gentamicin) is used as salvage therapy for SSNHL. High-yield pearl: SSNHL is a medical emergency — steroids must be started within 2 weeks for best outcomes. After 4–6 weeks, prognosis for recovery is poor. Exam trap: Do not confuse intratympanic dexamethasone (steroid — used in SSNHL salvage) with intratympanic gentamicin (aminoglycoside — used for Meniere's ablation).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old software engineer presents with recurrent episodic vertigo (each episode lasting 2–3 hours), left-sided fluctuating low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and aural fullness. He has had 6 episodes in the past 4 months. Audiometry shows a left-sided 'rising' sensorineural audiogram pattern (low-frequency loss). He has tried betahistine 16 mg TDS and a low-sodium diet for 6 months with no improvement. Electrocochleography (ECochG) shows a summating potential/action potential ratio >0.4. Which of the following is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: Add oral acetazolamide and continue conservative management
options.B: Intratympanic dexamethasone injection
options.C: Endolymphatic sac decompression surgery
options.D: Intratympanic gentamicin ablation

questions.explanation: This is Definite Meniere's Disease (AAO-HNS criteria: ≥2 episodes vertigo ≥20 min, audiometrically documented SNHL, ipsilateral tinnitus/aural fullness, not better accounted for by another diagnosis). ECochG SP/AP ratio >0.4 confirms endolymphatic hydrops. The patient has FAILED first-line treatment (betahistine + dietary modification ×6 months). Step-up approach in Meniere's: 1st line: Betahistine + low sodium diet → 2nd line: Intratympanic dexamethasone (steroid — preserves hearing) → 3rd line: Intratympanic gentamicin (chemical labyrinthectomy — ablates vestibular function, destroys hearing partially) → 4th line: Surgical (endolymphatic sac decompression, labyrinthectomy, vestibular neurectomy). Since he has already failed first-line, and assuming intratympanic dexamethasone was tried (the question implies adequate conservative failure), intratympanic gentamicin is the next step for unilateral disease. Option B (IT dexamethasone) would be correct if this were the immediate second step before gentamicin — but the question implies 6 months of conservative failure. In standard exam format, IT gentamicin is the answer for 'failed conservative management'. Option C (endolymphatic sac decompression): Evidence is weak (no better than sham surgery in randomised trials); not preferred over IT gentamicin in current practice. Option A: Acetazolamide has limited evidence in Meniere's. High-yield pearl: Intratympanic gentamicin preferentially destroys type I hair cells of the cristae, reducing vestibular input. Hearing loss is a risk (~15–20%). Used when vertigo control is priority and hearing is already poor. Exam trap: Low-frequency SNHL is the hallmark of Meniere's (opposite of noise-induced hearing loss which affects 4000 Hz).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old woman presents with sudden brief episodes of vertigo (lasting <1 minute) triggered by turning over in bed or looking up. She denies hearing loss, tinnitus, or neurological symptoms. The Dix-Hallpike test on the right side elicits upbeat-torsional nystagmus with a 5-second latency that fatigues on repeated testing. What is the MOST effective treatment?

options.A: Semont liberatory manoeuvre for left posterior canal BPPV
options.B: Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre for right posterior canal BPPV
options.C: Long-term betahistine 24 mg twice daily
options.D: MRI brain with gadolinium to rule out posterior fossa lesion

questions.explanation: This is classic posterior canal BPPV. Key diagnostic features: Brief (<1 min) positional vertigo, upbeat-torsional nystagmus on right Dix-Hallpike, latency of 5 seconds, fatigability. Positive right Dix-Hallpike = right posterior semicircular canal BPPV (affected ear is the one tested = side that is down). Treatment: Epley canalith repositioning manoeuvre for the affected ear (right side). This manoeuvres otoliths from the posterior canal back into the utricle via a series of head positions. Single-session success rate: ~80%. Option A: Semont manoeuvre is also used for posterior canal BPPV but is less commonly the 'most effective' first choice in standard exams; also, it would be for the RIGHT side (not left — this is a common trap). Option C: Betahistine is for Meniere's disease, not BPPV. It has no evidence in BPPV. Option D: MRI is not indicated when nystagmus is classic — upbeat-torsional, with latency and fatigability. Central vertigo (posterior fossa lesion) shows direction-changing, purely vertical nystagmus WITHOUT latency or fatigability. High-yield pearl: Upbeat-torsional nystagmus (top pole of eye beats toward the ground/affected side) = posterior canal BPPV. Geotropic horizontal nystagmus = horizontal canal BPPV. Exam trap: The affected ear in Dix-Hallpike is the ear that is LOWER (tested side), not the ear with nystagmus direction.

questions.question_text: A 48-year-old man presents with a 2-year history of progressive right-sided hearing loss, high-pitched tinnitus, and recent onset unsteadiness. He denies facial weakness or headache. Audiometry shows right-sided asymmetric SNHL with poor speech discrimination disproportionate to pure tone thresholds. An ABR shows prolonged wave I–V interpeak latency on the right. MRI with gadolinium shows the findings depicted in the image. The tumour measures 1.8 cm in its largest dimension. What is the MOST appropriate management for this patient?

options.A: Watchful waiting with annual MRI for 2 years
options.B: Translabyrinthine surgical resection
options.C: Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife)
options.D: Middle fossa craniotomy approach

questions.explanation: The image shows a classic vestibular schwannoma (acoustic neuroma): homogeneously enhancing CPA-IAC mass with 'ice cream cone' appearance (ball in cone = CPA component + IAC component). Tumour size 1.8 cm = small to medium-sized. Clinical features confirm the diagnosis: unilateral SNHL, poor speech discrimination, prolonged ABR wave I-V latency (retrocochlear pathology hallmark). For a 1.8 cm tumour in a 48-year-old: Stereotactic radiosurgery (Gamma Knife SRS) — excellent tumour control (>90% at 10 years), low risk of facial nerve injury, appropriate for tumours <3 cm without brainstem compression. Option A (watchful waiting): Appropriate only for elderly patients (>70 years), very small tumours (<1 cm), or those unfit for treatment. At 48 years with documented hearing loss and unsteadiness, active treatment is indicated. Option B (translabyrinthine): Provides widest exposure for large tumours; destroys residual hearing completely. Given the patient's tumour size (1.8 cm) and current hearing, less preferred unless hearing preservation is not a concern. Option D (middle fossa): Used for small intracanalicular tumours (<1 cm) with serviceable hearing and when hearing preservation is the goal. Not ideal at 1.8 cm with IAC + CPA extension. High-yield pearl: ABR/BAEP — prolonged wave I–V interpeak latency = hallmark of retrocochlear (VIII nerve) pathology. Most common CPA tumour = vestibular schwannoma (80%). Most common nerve of origin = superior vestibular nerve. Exam trap: 'Acoustic neuroma' is a misnomer — arises from vestibular nerve, not acoustic nerve; and is a Schwannoma, not a neuroma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman notices progressive bilateral hearing loss, worse during pregnancy. She speaks in a soft voice (paracusis Willisii). Her family history is positive for similar hearing loss. Otoscopy is normal. Pure tone audiometry shows bilateral conductive hearing loss with a characteristic notch at 2000 Hz. Tympanometry shows a Type As (shallow) curve with absent stapedial reflexes. What does the notch at 2000 Hz on the audiogram represent?

options.A: Carhart's notch — a mechanical artefact due to stapes fixation
options.B: Noise-induced hearing loss at high frequency
options.C: Cochlear dead region from endolymphatic hydrops
options.D: Neural dysfunction at the olivocochlear bundle

questions.explanation: This is classic otosclerosis: young woman, progressive bilateral conductive hearing loss, worsening with pregnancy (estrogen effect on spongiotic bone), positive family history (autosomal dominant, 25–40% penetrance), paracusis Willisii (paradoxical improvement in noisy environments due to others raising voice), normal otoscopy, absent stapedial reflexes, Type As tympanogram. The 2000 Hz notch on audiometry is called Carhart's notch — it is NOT a true sensorineural notch. It is a mechanical artefact caused by stapes fixation disturbing the resonance of the ossicular chain, which normally peaks near 2000 Hz. It disappears after successful stapedectomy. Option B: Noise-induced hearing loss characteristically causes a 4000 Hz notch (C5 dip), not 2000 Hz. Option C: Cochlear dead regions occur in Meniere's at low frequencies. Option D: Olivocochlear bundle dysfunction is not associated with audiometric notches. High-yield pearl: Otosclerosis histology — spongiotic bone replacing normal enchondral bone; surrounds the oval window (stapedial otosclerosis) most commonly. Blue mantle of Manasse seen histologically. Treatment: Stapedectomy (80–90% success) or hearing aid. Sodium fluoride may slow progression. Exam trap: Carhart's notch gives the false impression of sensorineural involvement — PTA with bone conduction shows an apparent notch at 2000 Hz even though cochlear function is normal. Post-stapedectomy, this notch resolves, confirming it was mechanical.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 72-year-old retired factory worker presents with bilateral gradual hearing loss for 5 years, worse in noisy environments. He has difficulty understanding speech, especially consonants, despite adequate loudness. His wife reports he often mishears words. Audiometry shows bilateral symmetrical high-frequency SNHL with sloping audiogram. He reports no tinnitus or vertigo. What is the MOST likely histopathological type of this patient's hearing loss?

options.A: Strial presbycusis — loss of stria vascularis cells with flat audiogram
options.B: Sensory presbycusis — loss of outer hair cells at basal turn with high-frequency sloping loss
options.C: Neural presbycusis — loss of spiral ganglion cells with disproportionate speech discrimination loss
options.D: Mechanical (cochlear conductive) presbycusis — stiffening of the basilar membrane

questions.explanation: Presbycusis (age-related SNHL) has 4 histopathological types (Schuknecht's classification): 1) Sensory — loss of outer hair cells at basal turn (high-frequency region); produces classic downward sloping audiogram; pure-tone thresholds correlate with speech discrimination. 2) Neural — loss of spiral ganglion cells; disproportionately poor speech discrimination relative to PTA thresholds; flat audiogram. 3) Strial (metabolic) — loss of stria vascularis (ion transport); flat audiogram across all frequencies; good speech discrimination for remaining thresholds. 4) Mechanical (cochlear conductive) — stiffening of basilar membrane; gradually sloping audiogram. This patient: Symmetrical high-frequency sloping audiogram + difficulty with consonants (high frequency sounds) = classic Sensory presbycusis. Option A (strial) = flat audiogram. Option C (neural) = poor speech discrimination out of proportion to PTA. Option D (mechanical) = gradually sloping. High-yield pearl: Most common type of presbycusis in exams is Sensory. Consonants (high frequency) are lost first — this is why patients say 'I can hear you speaking but can't understand what you say.' Exam trap: Noise-induced SNHL also shows high-frequency loss but is characterised by a 4000 Hz notch (C5 dip) and occupational/noise exposure history.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 65-year-old hypertensive man on warfarin (INR 3.8) presents to the emergency department with profuse right-sided epistaxis not controlled by pinching the nose for 20 minutes. On examination, blood is seen dripping posteriorly into the oropharynx. Anterior rhinoscopy shows no obvious bleeding point on Little's area. His blood pressure is 190/110 mmHg. He has undergone two failed anterior packing attempts. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: Bilateral anterior nasal packing with Merocel and IV tranexamic acid
options.B: Posterior nasal packing (Foley catheter or Brighton balloon) and IV vitamin K + FFP
options.C: Endoscopic sphenopalatine artery ligation immediately
options.D: External carotid artery ligation

questions.explanation: This patient has posterior epistaxis (blood dripping into oropharynx, no visible bleeding point in Little's area, failed anterior packing) compounded by supratherapeutic anticoagulation (INR 3.8) and uncontrolled hypertension. Immediate management: (1) Posterior nasal packing (Foley catheter inflated in nasopharynx with 8–10 mL saline, or Brighton balloon) to tamponade posterior bleeding. (2) Reversal of anticoagulation: IV Vitamin K (slow onset, 6–12 hrs) + Fresh Frozen Plasma (immediate effect) for INR 3.8 on warfarin. (3) Blood pressure control. Option A: Anterior packing has already failed twice and is inadequate for posterior epistaxis. Tranexamic acid has a role but is not sufficient alone. Option C (endoscopic SPA ligation): This is the preferred definitive surgical intervention for intractable posterior epistaxis, but only after initial packing has been attempted. If posterior packing also fails → proceed to endoscopic SPA ligation. Option D (ECA ligation): Largely replaced by endoscopic SPA ligation; used when endoscopic approach is not feasible. High-yield pearl: Sphenopalatine artery (branch of maxillary artery/ECA) supplies the posterior nasal cavity; it is the most common source of posterior epistaxis. Woodruff's plexus = posterior nasal bleeding site (compare to Kiesselbach's plexus = anterior/Little's area). Exam trap: In supratherapeutic INR, always reverse anticoagulation simultaneously with local control — packing without reversing coagulopathy will fail.

questions.question_text: A 38-year-old woman has recurrent episodes of right-sided facial pain, nasal obstruction, and mucopurulent nasal discharge for 18 months. She has received multiple courses of antibiotics without lasting relief. She completed a 12-week course of intranasal corticosteroids. CT PNS (coronal) shows the findings in the image above. Nasal endoscopy confirms bilateral nasal polyps (Grade II). What is the MOST appropriate definitive treatment?

options.A: Prolonged culture-directed antibiotics for 6 more weeks
options.B: Functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS)
options.C: Caldwell-Luc procedure for right maxillary sinus
options.D: Oral doxycycline 100 mg daily as anti-inflammatory for 3 months

questions.explanation: This is Chronic Rhinosinusitis with Nasal Polyps (CRSwNP), having failed adequate medical therapy (antibiotics + 12-week intranasal corticosteroids). The CT shows OMC obstruction and maxillary sinus opacification — the key anatomical target for surgery. FESS (Functional Endoscopic Sinus Surgery) is the definitive treatment for medically refractory CRS. It opens the osteomeatal complex, removes polyps, and restores mucociliary drainage. It is the gold standard. Option A: Prolonged antibiotics are useful in chronic sinusitis without polyps (e.g., macrolide therapy for its anti-inflammatory effect), but this patient has failed multiple antibiotics and has polyps — further antibiotics are inadequate. Option C (Caldwell-Luc): Extranasal approach to maxillary sinus, largely obsolete. Used only when endoscopic approach is impossible (severe anatomical distortion, failed FESS). The modern approach for maxillary sinus is middle meatal antrostomy via FESS. Option D: Low-dose macrolides (not doxycycline) have anti-inflammatory properties in CRS without polyps. Doxycycline is used in CRSwNP only in certain biological failure scenarios. High-yield pearl: Osteomeatal complex (OMC) is the key drainage pathway for frontal, maxillary, and anterior ethmoid sinuses. OMC obstruction = recurrent maxillary and frontal sinusitis. The OMC is the surgical target in FESS. Exam trap: Don't choose Caldwell-Luc — it is outdated and has higher morbidity. FESS is always preferred in modern practice.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man with known bronchial asthma presents with bilateral nasal polyps (confirmed on endoscopy), chronic rhinosinusitis, and a history of severe bronchospasm after taking aspirin for a headache. He underwent FESS 2 years ago but polyps have recurred. Serum eosinophil count is 1500/µL. What is the MOST appropriate next step in this patient's management?

options.A: Repeat FESS immediately with extended dissection
options.B: Subcutaneous dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα) therapy
options.C: Aspirin desensitisation protocol
options.D: Oral prednisolone 40 mg daily indefinitely

questions.explanation: This patient has Samter's Triad (Aspirin-Exacerbated Respiratory Disease — AERD): Asthma + Nasal polyps + Aspirin sensitivity. It is driven by eosinophilic inflammation (type 2 inflammation) mediated by IL-4, IL-5, IL-13. He has failed FESS (polyp recurrence) = medically and surgically refractory CRSwNP. Dupilumab: Biologic agent (monoclonal antibody against IL-4 receptor alpha); blocks both IL-4 and IL-13 signalling; FDA/EMA approved for severe CRSwNP as add-on maintenance therapy in adults who are not adequately controlled with intranasal corticosteroids. Indicated specifically for eosinophilic CRSwNP (eosinophils >1500/µL = strong indicator). Option A (repeat FESS): Previous FESS failed with recurrence — indicates aggressive type 2 inflammation; a second FESS without addressing the underlying biology is unlikely to provide lasting benefit. Option C (Aspirin desensitisation): Valid option in AERD to reduce polyp recurrence, but not as effective as biologics and has significant side effects; NOT the first choice after surgical failure in an era of biologics. Option D (indefinite oral steroids): Highly effective for short-term polyp reduction but indefinite use is inappropriate due to systemic side effects (diabetes, osteoporosis, adrenal suppression). Used for short rescue courses only. High-yield pearl: AERD involves overproduction of cysteinyl leukotrienes due to COX-1 inhibition by aspirin, shunting arachidonic acid to the 5-LOX pathway. Key: No NSAIDs/COX-1 inhibitors in AERD. Safe analgesic = paracetamol (weak COX-2 preferential). Exam trap: Do not confuse eosinophilic CRS (type 2, polyps, responds to dupilumab) with neutrophilic CRS (type 1, no polyps, responds to macrolides).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old medical student presents with 3 years of perennial nasal symptoms: sneezing, watery rhinorrhoea, nasal itching, and bilateral nasal obstruction, worse during exams. She also has itching of the eyes. Skin prick testing is positive for house dust mite (HDM). She is currently using oral cetirizine 10 mg daily and intranasal fluticasone with partial relief. What is the MOST effective long-term disease-modifying treatment for her condition?

options.A: Montelukast (leukotriene receptor antagonist) added to existing regimen
options.B: Allergen Immunotherapy (AIT) with house dust mite extracts
options.C: Intranasal azelastine (antihistamine nasal spray)
options.D: Omalizumab (anti-IgE biologic) subcutaneous injection

questions.explanation: Allergen Immunotherapy (AIT) is the ONLY disease-modifying treatment for allergic rhinitis. It desensitizes the immune system by inducing regulatory T cells, shifting Th2 to Th1 response, and reducing mast cell/basophil reactivity. Available as SCIT (subcutaneous) or SLIT (sublingual). For confirmed HDM allergy (positive SPT) with inadequate symptom control on standard pharmacotherapy (antihistamine + INCS), AIT is the next step. Benefits persist for years after completing a 3-year course. Option A (montelukast): Provides symptomatic relief (nasal blockage, especially in AR+asthma) but does NOT modify the underlying allergic disease. It is additive symptomatic therapy, not disease-modifying. Option C (intranasal azelastine): Symptomatic relief only; no disease modification. Option D (omalizumab): Anti-IgE biologic; approved for severe allergic asthma and chronic urticaria; not currently the first-choice add-on for allergic rhinitis alone (though used off-label). Much more expensive than AIT. High-yield pearl: AIT is the only treatment that can potentially cure allergic rhinitis — symptoms can remain reduced for years after stopping. All other drugs (antihistamines, INCS, leukotriene antagonists) are symptomatic only. Exam trap: AIT is indicated AFTER pharmacotherapy has failed, not as first-line. Contraindications include severe/uncontrolled asthma and autoimmune disease.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 16-year-old boy presents with progressive left-sided nasal obstruction and recurrent episodes of profuse, spontaneous, non-traumatic epistaxis for 8 months. Examination shows a pale, firm, non-tender nasopharyngeal mass. CT scan shows a lobulated, enhancing mass centred at the sphenopalatine foramen extending into the pterygopalatine fossa and nasal cavity. MRI shows flow voids within the mass. What is the investigation of choice to plan definitive management?

options.A: Diagnostic endoscopic biopsy under local anaesthesia
options.B: Contrast-enhanced CT of neck to identify lymph node involvement
options.C: Digital subtraction angiography (DSA) and pre-operative embolisation
options.D: Fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) of the nasopharyngeal mass

questions.explanation: This is a classic Juvenile Nasopharyngeal Angiofibroma (JNA): adolescent male, progressive nasal obstruction, recurrent spontaneous profuse epistaxis, sphenopalatine foramen centred enhancing mass, MRI flow voids (highly vascular). JNA is a histologically benign but locally aggressive vascular tumour. BIOPSY IS CONTRAINDICATED — risk of catastrophic haemorrhage due to extreme vascularity. Investigation of choice: Digital Subtraction Angiography (DSA) which (1) delineates vascular supply (typically sphenopalatine artery + ascending pharyngeal artery), (2) allows therapeutic pre-operative embolisation 24–48 hours before surgery to reduce intraoperative blood loss. Definitive treatment: Surgical excision (endoscopic or open depending on stage). Embolisation alone is NOT curative. Option A (biopsy): Absolutely contraindicated in JNA due to risk of life-threatening haemorrhage. Option B (CT neck): Not needed — JNA rarely involves cervical lymph nodes (it is benign). Option D (FNAC): Contraindicated for the same reason as biopsy. High-yield pearl: JNA is the most common benign nasopharyngeal tumour in adolescent males. It arises from fibrovascular stroma near the sphenopalatine foramen. Biopsy is ALWAYS contraindicated. Antral sign (Holman-Miller sign) on lateral X-ray: anterior bowing of the posterior wall of the maxillary antrum. Exam trap: 'What investigation to plan management?' = DSA for embolisation. 'What investigation to confirm diagnosis?' = CT/MRI (clinical diagnosis; histology confirms post-excision).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man presents with clear, unilateral right-sided watery nasal discharge that increases when he bends forward. He had a road traffic accident 3 months ago with head injury requiring hospitalisation. The discharge tests positive for beta-2 transferrin. CT PNS shows a defect in the cribriform plate. He has had 2 episodes of bacterial meningitis since the head injury. What is the MOST appropriate definitive treatment?

options.A: Lumbar puncture and CSF pressure measurement followed by acetazolamide
options.B: Prophylactic antibiotics and observation for 6 months
options.C: Endoscopic endonasal repair of the cribriform plate defect
options.D: External frontoethmoidectomy approach for repair

questions.explanation: This patient has traumatic CSF rhinorrhoea from a cribriform plate defect, confirmed by: (1) clear unilateral watery discharge increasing with bending (orthostatically-dependent), (2) beta-2 transferrin positive (gold standard test for CSF), (3) CT showing cribriform plate defect, (4) recurrent meningitis (absolute indication for surgical repair). Beta-2 transferrin: Highly specific (96%) and sensitive (99%) for CSF. It is present in CSF, perilymph, and aqueous humour but NOT in nasal secretions or blood. Definitive treatment: Endoscopic endonasal repair — uses fat, fascia lata, or mucosal flap to seal the defect. This has replaced open approaches due to lower morbidity, direct visualisation, and excellent success rates (>90%). Option A (acetazolamide): Reduces CSF production; used only for idiopathic intracranial hypertension-related CSF rhinorrhoea or as temporary measure. In traumatic CSF leak with recurrent meningitis, surgical closure is mandatory. Option B (prophylactic antibiotics): Evidence shows antibiotics do NOT prevent meningitis in CSF leaks and may select resistant organisms. Observation is only acceptable for small leaks that may close spontaneously (within 2 weeks). This patient has had 2 meningitis episodes — observation is no longer appropriate. Option D (external frontoethmoidectomy): Obsolete for cribriform plate repair; endoscopic approach is far superior with less morbidity. High-yield pearl: Halo sign (ring of clear fluid around blood on gauze) = field test for CSF; not reliable. Beta-2 transferrin = gold standard. Exam trap: Never give prophylactic antibiotics for CSF rhinorrhoea — no evidence, may cause resistant meningitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with progressive nasal crusting, epistaxis, and nasal obstruction for 1 year. She also has haemoptysis, haematuria, and peripheral oedema. Examination reveals saddle-nose deformity, septal perforation, and bilateral lower limb oedema. Urinalysis shows red cell casts and proteinuria. CXR shows bilateral pulmonary infiltrates. Blood tests: cANCA (PR3-ANCA) strongly positive, creatinine 240 µmol/L. What is the MOST appropriate treatment?

options.A: Long-term doxycycline 100 mg daily
options.B: Rituximab infusion and systemic corticosteroids
options.C: Oral metronidazole and nasal saline irrigation
options.D: FESS and intravenous fluconazole

questions.explanation: This is Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis (GPA / Wegener's Granulomatosis): classic triad of (1) upper respiratory tract (nasal/sinus involvement: saddle nose, septal perforation, crusting), (2) lower respiratory tract (pulmonary infiltrates, haemoptysis), (3) renal involvement (glomerulonephritis: red cell casts, proteinuria, elevated creatinine). cANCA (PR3-ANCA) positive = confirmatory. This is a systemic vasculitis requiring immunosuppressive therapy. Treatment: Induction — Rituximab (anti-CD20 monoclonal antibody, preferred in AAV per RAVE trial) or Cyclophosphamide + high-dose systemic corticosteroids. Maintenance — Rituximab or azathioprine. Option A (doxycycline): No role in GPA. Some older theories suggested Staphylococcus trigger for GPA, but antibiotic monotherapy is completely inadequate for this systemic vasculitis with renal involvement. Option C (metronidazole + saline): Saline irrigation is used for symptomatic nasal care in GPA but is NOT definitive treatment. Option D (FESS + fluconazole): FESS may be used for sinus disease in GPA, but fluconazole suggests fungal disease, which is not the diagnosis here. High-yield pearl: Saddle nose deformity = destruction of the nasal cartilage/septum; causes: GPA, relapsing polychondritis, leprosy, syphilis, cocaine abuse, trauma. ANCA types: cANCA (PR3) = GPA. pANCA (MPO) = Microscopic Polyangiitis (MPA) and Eosinophilic GPA (EGPA/Churg-Strauss). Exam trap: EGPA (Churg-Strauss) also causes nasal polyps + asthma + eosinophilia + pANCA. GPA = cANCA + renal involvement + NO asthma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: An 8-year-old girl has had 7 episodes of documented acute tonsillitis requiring antibiotics in the past 12 months (4 in one year, 3 in the previous year). She misses school frequently. She does not have obstructive sleep symptoms. Throat swabs have grown Group A Streptococcus on 4 occasions. Her parents are asking about tonsillectomy. Based on the Paradise criteria, what is the MOST appropriate advice?

options.A: Tonsillectomy is not yet indicated; wait until she has 7 episodes in a single calendar year
options.B: Tonsillectomy is indicated as she meets the modified Paradise criteria
options.C: Prophylactic penicillin V for 12 months should be tried before surgery
options.D: Adenotonsillectomy is preferred over tonsillectomy alone in all children

questions.explanation: Paradise Criteria for tonsillectomy (recurrent acute tonsillitis): 7+ episodes in 1 year, OR 5+ episodes/year for 2 consecutive years, OR 3+ episodes/year for 3 consecutive years. Each episode must include: fever >38.3°C, cervical lymphadenopathy, tonsillar exudate, or positive streptococcal culture. This child: 4 episodes last year + 3 episodes this year (12 months) = total 7 in 2 years, meeting the '5+/year for 2 years' criterion. Tonsillectomy is indicated. Option A: The criterion is NOT 7 in a single calendar year — this is a common exam misconception. Paradise criteria includes '5+ per year for 2 years' which this child meets. Option C: Long-term prophylactic penicillin may reduce recurrences but is not standard care when surgical criteria are met. Side effects (GI, allergy) and poor compliance make this less preferred. Option D: Adenotonsillectomy is preferred in children with obstructive sleep apnoea. This child has NO obstructive symptoms, so tonsillectomy alone is appropriate. High-yield pearl: Paradise criteria = most widely used clinical guideline for tonsillectomy in recurrent tonsillitis. Document each episode carefully — fever, lymphadenopathy, exudate, or culture. Obstructive sleep apnoea = separate indication for adenotonsillectomy (not Paradise criteria). Exam trap: Many candidates remember '7 episodes' but forget the alternative: '5 per year × 2 years' OR '3 per year × 3 years'.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 22-year-old man presents with 5-day history of severe sore throat, difficulty swallowing, and inability to open his mouth fully. Examination reveals a hot potato voice, drooling, uvular deviation to the right, left peritonsillar bulging with erythema, and trismus (mouth opening 1.5 cm). Temperature 38.9°C. What is the MOST appropriate immediate management?

options.A: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate and warm saline gargles
options.B: IV corticosteroids and empirical IV antibiotics, with needle aspiration of the abscess
options.C: Emergency tonsillectomy (quinsy tonsillectomy) under general anaesthesia
options.D: CT neck with contrast to rule out deep neck space infection before any intervention

questions.explanation: This is a peritonsillar abscess (quinsy): hallmark features — unilateral peritonsillar bulging, uvular deviation to opposite side, trismus (medial pterygoid spasm), hot potato voice (muffled from pharyngeal swelling), drooling (dysphagia), fever. MOST COMMON complication of tonsillitis. Management: (1) IV antibiotics (benzylpenicillin + metronidazole, or amoxicillin-clavulanate) — for anaerobes and streptococcus. (2) IV corticosteroids (dexamethasone 10 mg) — reduce swelling and improve trismus/pain rapidly. (3) Drainage: Needle aspiration (75–85% cure, can be done under local anaesthesia) OR incision and drainage (I&D). Needle aspiration is first line in most centres; I&D is done if aspiration fails. Option A: Oral antibiotics are inadequate for an established abscess — needs drainage. Option C: Quinsy tonsillectomy (interval tonsillectomy) is performed 4–6 weeks AFTER resolution of acute episode, or acutely in patients with recurrent abscesses or airway concern. Not first-line for a first episode. Option D: CT neck is indicated if deep neck space infection is suspected (worsening despite drainage, signs of Ludwig's angina, parapharyngeal/retropharyngeal spread). Not required before initial drainage of a straightforward quinsy. High-yield pearl: Quinsy = peritonsillar abscess. Uvular deviation = AWAY from the side of the abscess. Trismus = medial pterygoid spasm (quinsy tip). Parapharyngeal space is the most common site of spread from quinsy. Exam trap: Peritonsillar cellulitis (no abscess) = antibiotics only, no drainage. Quinsy (abscess) = drainage + antibiotics. CT helps distinguish these when clinical doubt exists.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old poorly controlled diabetic man presents with fever, dysphagia, drooling, and progressive neck swelling for 4 days. He had a dental extraction 1 week ago. Examination shows bilateral brawny submandibular swelling, elevation and posterior displacement of the tongue, stridor, and cannot open mouth beyond 1 cm. Temperature 39.5°C, SpO2 93% on room air. CT neck shows bilateral submandibular and sublingual space gas-forming infection with extension to the parapharyngeal space. What is the MOST appropriate first step?

options.A: Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics and close monitoring in HDU
options.B: Emergency tracheotomy under local anaesthesia, followed by wide neck drainage
options.C: Orotracheal intubation by rapid sequence induction and immediate surgical drainage
options.D: Needle aspiration of submandibular swelling and IV meropenem

questions.explanation: This is Ludwig's Angina — a life-threatening, rapidly spreading bilateral cellulitis/fasciitis of the submandibular, sublingual, and submental spaces, typically from a dental source. Hallmarks: Bilateral submandibular/sublingual swelling, woody brawny induration (not fluctuant = cellulitis, not abscess), tongue elevation and posterior displacement, stridor, difficulty swallowing, SpO2 93% (impending respiratory failure), gas-forming infection on CT (anaerobes). The PRIORITY is AIRWAY — it is a true surgical emergency with 50% mortality if airway is lost. Airway management: Awake fibreoptic intubation or surgical tracheotomy under local anaesthesia — NOT rapid sequence orotracheal intubation. Reason: The oropharynx is severely distorted and oedematous. Direct laryngoscopy/RSI risks complete airway loss if intubation fails (cannot ventilate, cannot intubate scenario). Tracheotomy under local anaesthesia with sedation is safest when RSI is not feasible. Option A: Antibiotics alone are inadequate — established gas-forming deep space infection with airway compromise requires surgical drainage. Option C: RSI risks 'cannot intubate, cannot oxygenate' scenario in distorted airway. Option D: Ludwig's is a cellulitis, not an abscess — needle aspiration will yield nothing. Systemic antibiotics are essential but secondary to airway management. High-yield pearl: Ludwig's Angina mnemonic = Bilateral, Brawny, Board-like induration (not fluctuant), Bilateral submandibular + sublingual + submental spaces. Most common source: lower molar dental infection (especially 2nd/3rd mandibular molar). Most common organisms: polymicrobial, anaerobes (Bacteroides, Fusobacterium) + Streptococcus. Exam trap: Do not attempt orotracheal intubation in Ludwig's with severe swelling without fibreoptic guidance or surgical backup.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old male, 40 pack-year smoker, presents with progressive hoarseness of 4 months duration. He denies dysphagia, neck swelling, or haemoptysis. Flexible laryngoscopy reveals a white, irregular lesion confined to the right true vocal cord (TVC) with normal cord mobility. Biopsy shows moderately differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. CT neck/chest shows no lymph node involvement and no distant metastasis. Staging: T1a N0 M0 glottic SCC. What is the treatment that BEST preserves voice quality while achieving cure?

options.A: Total laryngectomy
options.B: Radiotherapy alone (66 Gy in 33 fractions)
options.C: Transoral laser microsurgery (TLM) — endoscopic CO2 laser cordectomy
options.D: Partial laryngectomy (vertical hemilaryngectomy)

questions.explanation: T1a glottic SCC = tumour limited to one true vocal cord with normal mobility. Treatment options for T1a glottic SCC: (1) Transoral Laser Microsurgery (TLM) — endoscopic CO2 laser cordectomy, and (2) Radiotherapy. Both have equivalent cure rates (>90% 5-year local control). However, the question asks what BEST PRESERVES voice quality while achieving cure. TLM advantages: Single outpatient procedure, no radiation side effects (xerostomia, radiation mucositis, risk of hypothyroidism, rare chondronecrosis), lower long-term morbidity, cost-effective, can be repeated if local recurrence, and preserves residual vocal fold tissue. Voice outcomes are excellent for superficial lesions. Radiotherapy: Also curative but requires 6–7 weeks of daily treatment, radiation side effects, and voice quality depends on radiation response. For early T1a glottic SCC, TLM is now preferred in most high-volume centres. Option A (total laryngectomy): Used for T3/T4 tumours or salvage after failed chemoradiation. Completely inappropriate for T1a. Option D (partial/hemilaryngectomy): Open surgical approach; higher morbidity than TLM; reserved when TLM is not feasible. High-yield pearl: Glottic tumours present early (hoarseness) because vocal cords have poor lymphatic drainage → T1 glottic tumours = excellent prognosis. Supraglottic tumours present late with dysphagia/neck nodes (rich lymphatics). Exam trap: Many candidates choose radiotherapy assuming it always gives better voice. Modern evidence shows TLM achieves equivalent cure with faster recovery and comparable/better voice for early glottic SCC.

questions.subject: ENT
key_findings: Thumb sign — enlarged epiglottis resembling a thumb print
Loss of normal vallecula air space
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old unimmunised child is brought to the emergency department with high fever (40°C), sudden-onset severe sore throat, drooling, dysphagia, and inspiratory stridor. He is sitting upright in the tripod position and appears toxic and anxious. His voice is muffled. The lateral neck X-ray shows the finding depicted in the image. What is the MOST critical next step?

options.A: Immediate oropharyngeal examination with a tongue depressor to assess epiglottis
options.B: IV ceftriaxone and dexamethasone and close monitoring
options.C: Secure the airway in the operating theatre under controlled conditions
options.D: Flexible nasendoscopy in the emergency room to confirm diagnosis

questions.explanation: This is classic acute epiglottitis (supraglottitis): Unimmunised child (Haemophilus influenzae type b is the classic pathogen), high fever, toxic appearance, drooling (cannot swallow), tripod position (extends airway), muffled 'hot potato' voice, inspiratory stridor. Lateral neck X-ray: Thumb sign = massively swollen epiglottis. This is a life-threatening ENT emergency. AIRWAY IS THE PRIORITY. The child must go to the operating theatre IMMEDIATELY where an experienced anaesthetist and ENT surgeon are both present. Inhalational induction of anaesthesia (with sevoflurane) is used → intubation under direct vision. Tracheotomy is set up as backup. Option A: DO NOT ATTEMPT OROPHARYNGEAL EXAMINATION WITH A TONGUE DEPRESSOR in the emergency room — this can trigger complete laryngospasm and precipitate fatal airway obstruction. Option B: Antibiotics + steroids are essential treatment BUT airway must be secured FIRST. Never give IV antibiotics and just observe — the airway can obstruct at any moment. Option D: Flexible nasendoscopy in the ED is risky — any stimulation can precipitate laryngospasm; should only be attempted in adults or in an extremely controlled setting. High-yield pearl: Epiglottitis vs Croup: Epiglottitis = supraglottic (H. influenzae type b), toxic, no cough, no barking, drooling, thumb sign. Croup = subglottic (parainfluenza), barking cough, steeple sign on AP X-ray. After Hib vaccination: epiglottitis now more common in adults (Streptococcus, Staphylococcus). Exam trap: NEVER examine the throat of a suspected epiglottitis patient outside the controlled OR setting.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 58-year-old man is referred for hoarseness of voice for 3 months. He underwent a left total thyroidectomy 4 months ago for thyroid cancer. Flexible laryngoscopy confirms left true vocal cord palsy — the left TVC is fixed in the paramedian position. He also has a bovine cough and aspiration of liquids. CT chest shows no recurrent tumour. Laryngeal electromyography (EMG) shows absence of electrical activity in the left thyroarytenoid muscle. He has significant dysphonia affecting his work as a lawyer. What is the MOST appropriate intervention for voice improvement?

options.A: Voice therapy with speech language pathologist for 6 months before any procedure
options.B: Left arytenoidectomy to lateralise the vocal cord
options.C: Left medialization laryngoplasty (thyroplasty Type I)
options.D: Botulinum toxin injection into the right (normal) vocal cord

questions.explanation: Left RLN palsy post-thyroidectomy with cord fixed in paramedian position. EMG shows denervation (absent electrical activity) = complete RLN injury, unlikely to recover spontaneously. The patient has dysphonia + aspiration (liquids), significantly affecting quality of life as a lawyer. For a PERMANENT unilateral vocal cord palsy (EMG showing denervation, 4+ months elapsed, no recovery expected): Medialization laryngoplasty (Thyroplasty Type I) — a silastic or hydroxyapatite implant is placed through a window in the thyroid cartilage to push the paralysed cord medially, allowing the normal cord to meet it during phonation. This is a permanent voice improvement procedure. Option A: Voice therapy alone is inadequate for aspiration and significant dysphonia when cord is permanently denervated. A short course of voice therapy is appropriate initially (especially for temporary palsy <6 months), but at 4 months with clear denervation on EMG, surgical intervention is more appropriate for this high-demand professional. Option B (arytenoidectomy/lateralisation): This LATERALISES the cord further — used for bilateral VCP to improve airway. In unilateral VCP, this would WORSEN the voice and increase aspiration. Option D (Botox into normal cord): This weakens the normal cord — used in spasmodic dysphonia (hyperadduction), NOT appropriate here. High-yield pearl: Unilateral VCP management by time course: <6 months = voice therapy + injection augmentation (temporary, e.g., Gelfoam). >6 months with denervation = Thyroplasty Type I (permanent medialization). Bilateral VCP (both cords medial) = bilateral arytenoidectomy or cord lateralisation to improve AIRWAY. Exam trap: Arytenoidectomy = airway procedure (lateralises cord). Thyroplasty = voice procedure (medialises cord). These are OPPOSITE movements with OPPOSITE indications.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 70-year-old woman presents with progressive dysphagia to solids for 6 months, now also affecting liquids. She regurgitates undigested food, especially at night, and has a history of intermittent neck gurgling. She has lost 8 kg. Barium swallow shows a posterior pharyngeal pouch at the Killian's dehiscence with contrast pooling. Rigid oesophagoscopy confirms a Zenker's diverticulum of 4 cm. What is the MOST appropriate surgical treatment?

options.A: Open transcervical diverticulectomy alone
options.B: Endoscopic stapler diverticulotomy (Dohlman-Holinger procedure with linear stapler)
options.C: Watchful waiting as surgery has high aspiration risk in elderly
options.D: Botulinum toxin injection into the cricopharyngeus muscle

questions.explanation: Zenker's diverticulum: False (pulsion) diverticulum formed by herniation of pharyngeal mucosa posteriorly through Killian's dehiscence (triangle between inferior pharyngeal constrictor and cricopharyngeus muscle). Symptoms: Dysphagia, regurgitation of undigested food, neck gurgling, halitosis, aspiration, weight loss. Key: The cricopharyngeus muscle dysfunction is the primary pathophysiology — the diverticulum forms SECONDARY to a hypertensive UES (cricopharyngeal dysfunction). Treatment options: 1. Endoscopic stapler diverticulotomy (Dohlman procedure + linear stapler): Cuts the common wall between the diverticulum and the oesophagus (including cricopharyngeus) using an endoscopic linear stapler. Minimally invasive, short anaesthesia, excellent results, low complication rate, preferred in elderly/high-risk patients for >3 cm diverticula. 2. Open transcervical diverticulectomy + cricopharyngeal myotomy: Traditional approach; higher morbidity (fistula, recurrent nerve injury) but done when endoscopic approach is not feasible. Option A: Diverticulectomy ALONE without myotomy of cricopharyngeus leads to high recurrence because the underlying muscle dysfunction is not addressed. Option C: Watchful waiting is inappropriate — the patient has significant dysphagia, aspiration risk from regurgitation, and weight loss. Option D: Botox injection into cricopharyngeus temporarily relaxes the muscle but does not address the diverticulum; relief is temporary (3–6 months) and mainly used in high-risk patients unfit for any procedure. High-yield pearl: Zenker's is a FALSE diverticulum (mucosa + submucosa only; no muscle layer). Location: Posterior midline through Killian's dehiscence. Killian's triangle = between thyropharyngeus and cricopharyngeus portions of inferior constrictor. Exam trap: Pulsion diverticulum (Zenker's) is most common pharyngeal diverticulum and arises ABOVE the cricopharyngeus. Do not confuse with epiphrenic diverticulum (at lower oesophagus, associated with achalasia).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old obese man (BMI 38 kg/m²) presents with daytime somnolence (Epworth Sleepiness Scale 16/24), loud snoring, and witnessed apnoeic episodes by his wife. He has poorly controlled hypertension and type 2 diabetes. Overnight polysomnography (PSG) shows an Apnoea-Hypopnoea Index (AHI) of 42 events/hour with oxygen desaturations to SpO2 72%. He is a truck driver. What is the MOST appropriate first-line treatment?

options.A: Uvulopalatopharyngoplasty (UPPP) surgery
options.B: Mandibular advancement device (MAD)
options.C: Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) therapy
options.D: Weight loss programme and positional therapy

questions.explanation: This is Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnoea (OSA): AHI = 42 events/hour (severe = AHI >30), SpO2 nadir 72%, ESS 16 (severe daytime somnolence), obesity, comorbidities (hypertension, T2DM), professional driver (road safety risk). Treatment of choice for moderate-severe OSA: CPAP (Continuous Positive Airway Pressure) therapy. CPAP is the gold standard first-line treatment for moderate (AHI 15–30) and severe (AHI >30) OSA. It provides a pneumatic splint keeping the upper airway open throughout sleep. Benefits: Reduces AHI to <5, improves SpO2, reduces daytime sleepiness, lowers blood pressure, reduces cardiovascular events, improves diabetes control, reduces road accident risk. Option A (UPPP): Surgery for OSA is second-line after CPAP failure; less effective for severe OSA (cure rate <50%); useful for palatal-level obstruction in selected cases. Option B (MAD): Mandibular advancement device is used for mild-moderate OSA or CPAP-intolerant patients; less effective for severe OSA. Option D (Weight loss + positional therapy): Adjunct measures, not sufficient as primary treatment for severe OSA with AHI 42, critical hypoxia (SpO2 72%), and professional driving risk. High-yield pearl: AHI classification: Mild = 5–15, Moderate = 15–30, Severe = >30 events/hour. CPAP compliance is key; heated humidification improves adherence. Epworth Sleepiness Scale (ESS): >10 = excessive daytime sleepiness. Exam trap: MAD is used for mild-moderate OSA when CPAP is not tolerated. For severe OSA (AHI 42, SpO2 72%), CPAP is mandatory, especially in a professional driver with road safety implications.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with a 3-month history of a painless, firm right neck lump at Level II (jugulodigastric region). He denies hoarseness, dysphagia, epistaxis, or otalgia. He is a non-smoker. Examination shows a 3 × 2 cm, non-tender, firm lymph node. Oropharyngeal and nasopharyngeal examination is unremarkable. FNAC of the neck node shows poorly differentiated squamous cell carcinoma. Panendoscopy under GA reveals no primary tumour. EBV serology is elevated. PET-CT identifies FDG uptake in the right neck node only, with a suspicious area in the right palatine tonsil. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: Bilateral tonsillectomy and base of tongue mucosal biopsies
options.B: Right radical neck dissection and ipsilateral radiotherapy
options.C: Empirical chemoradiation to the bilateral neck and nasopharynx
options.D: Repeat FNAC with HPV p16 immunostaining

questions.explanation: This is a classic 'unknown primary' head and neck squamous cell carcinoma (UPSCC) scenario with a neck node (Level II) and suspicious PET-CT signal in the right tonsil. In SCC of unknown primary in the head and neck, the protocol is: (1) PET-CT to identify likely primary site. (2) Panendoscopy under GA with directed biopsies. (3) If no primary found on panendoscopy: Bilateral tonsillectomy + base of tongue mucosectomy or biopsies — this identifies the primary in up to 40–70% of UPSCC cases (HPV-associated tonsillar or BOT primary in this age group with elevated EBV serology). Finding the primary changes staging and allows targeted treatment, potentially avoiding wide-field radiation. Option B: Radical neck dissection + radiotherapy without identifying primary would mean treating empirically; finding the primary allows precise radiation field planning. Option C: Empirical chemoradiation before identifying primary means unnecessary wide-field bilateral mucosal irradiation with increased toxicity. Option D: p16 immunostaining on existing FNAC material is useful (p16+ = HPV-related SCC) and should be done, but is not the MOST IMPORTANT next step for locating the primary and planning treatment. High-yield pearl: HPV-associated OPSCC: p16 positive, younger patients, good prognosis, Level II/III nodes, often from tonsil or BOT. EBV-associated SCC: nasopharyngeal carcinoma. Exam trap: PET-CT suspicious area in tonsil = strong indication for bilateral tonsillectomy (occult primary may be microscopic, missed on surface biopsy). Bilateral because occult primaries can be contralateral to the neck node.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman presents with a 2-year history of a slow-growing painless left parotid mass. She has no facial weakness. FNAC shows a biphasic pattern of epithelial cells forming ducts and myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid stroma. The tumour is well-defined, 3 cm, confined to the superficial lobe. What is the MOST appropriate treatment?

options.A: Enucleation of the tumour alone
options.B: Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve preservation
options.C: Total parotidectomy with facial nerve sacrifice
options.D: Radiotherapy alone as the tumour is benign

questions.explanation: FNAC findings describe a Pleomorphic Adenoma (benign mixed tumour) — biphasic pattern with epithelial/duct-forming cells and myoepithelial cells in a chondromyxoid stroma. Most common benign salivary gland tumour (70% of parotid tumours). Risk: Malignant transformation to carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma (5–10% over 15+ years). Treatment: Superficial parotidectomy with facial nerve identification and preservation. This removes the tumour with an adequate cuff of normal parotid tissue, reducing recurrence risk to <5%. The facial nerve runs through the parotid gland and must be identified and preserved. Option A (enucleation): Associated with very high recurrence rates (20–40%) due to incomplete removal of satellite nodules and pseudopodia that breach the capsule. Strictly CONTRAINDICATED for pleomorphic adenoma. Option C (total parotidectomy + facial nerve sacrifice): Appropriate for malignant parotid tumours invading the facial nerve. Not indicated for a benign superficial lobe tumour — facial nerve is preserved unless directly invaded. Option D: Radiotherapy has no role as primary treatment for benign parotid tumours. It is used as adjuvant treatment after inadequate resection of malignant tumours. High-yield pearl: Rule of 80s for parotid lumps: 80% of salivary gland tumours are in the parotid; 80% of parotid tumours are benign; 80% of benign parotid tumours are pleomorphic adenomas. Most common salivary gland malignancy: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (overall); Adenoid cystic carcinoma (submandibular/minor glands). Exam trap: Pleomorphic adenoma → NEVER enucleate. Warthin's tumour (papillary cystadenoma lymphomatosum) = bilateral in 10%, associated with smoking, bilateral parotid, oncocytic cells + lymphoid stroma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman is referred with a 2 cm right thyroid nodule found incidentally on neck ultrasound. She is clinically euthyroid. Ultrasound shows a solid hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins, microcalcifications (punctate), and increased internal vascularity (Doppler). FNAC (Bethesda system): Category V — Suspicious for malignancy. Which feature on ultrasound is MOST associated with malignancy in thyroid nodules?

options.A: Purely cystic appearance with anechoic content
options.B: Peripheral 'eggshell' calcification
options.C: Microcalcifications (punctate calcifications)
options.D: Hyperechoic nodule with a complete halo sign

questions.explanation: Ultrasound features of thyroid nodules and their malignancy risk: HIGH-RISK features (strongly associated with malignancy): Microcalcifications (punctate) — most specific for papillary thyroid cancer (psammoma bodies); Irregular/spiculated margins; Hypoechoic relative to strap muscles; Taller-than-wide shape (greater AP than transverse dimension); Evidence of extrathyroidal extension. INTERMEDIATE risk: Solid composition; Increased internal vascularity. LOW-RISK features: Purely cystic (almost always benign); Spongiform appearance (honeycomb pattern); Isoechoic or hyperechoic. Option A (purely cystic): Lowest malignancy risk (<1%). Option B (peripheral eggshell calcification): Benign pattern in older literature; however, recent data suggests interrupted eggshell calcification carries moderate malignancy risk. Complete peripheral calcification is traditionally considered benign (dystrophic calcification from healed multinodular goitre). Option D (hyperechoic with halo): Halo sign = peripheral hypoechoic rim (represents pseudocapsule); hyperechoic nodule = lower risk than hypoechoic. High-yield pearl: Bethesda Category V (Suspicious for Malignancy) = 60–75% risk of malignancy → surgery (diagnostic lobectomy or total thyroidectomy). Bethesda Category VI (Malignant) = >97% → total thyroidectomy. Microcalcifications = psammoma bodies = papillary thyroid carcinoma (most common thyroid malignancy, excellent prognosis). Exam trap: Calcifications in thyroid: Microcalcifications = malignant (papillary cancer). Macrocalcifications/peripheral calcifications = benign (old colloid nodule/multinodular goitre).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 3-year-old child presents with 2 days of right ear pain, fever (38.8°C), and pulling at the right ear. He had an upper respiratory tract infection 1 week ago. Otoscopy shows a red, bulging, non-perforated right tympanic membrane with reduced mobility. He attends daycare. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Watchful waiting for 72 hours with analgesics only
options.B: Amoxicillin 90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 10 days
options.C: Amoxicillin-clavulanate 90 mg/kg/day for 10 days
options.D: Immediate myringotomy

questions.explanation: This is Acute Otitis Media (AOM) in a child <2 years (actually 3 years, but with severe features). Per AAO-HNS / NICE guidelines, antibiotic treatment is recommended when: Age <6 months (always treat), Bilateral AOM in age <2 years, Severe symptoms (fever ≥39°C, severe otalgia), OR otorrhoea, OR failed watchful waiting. This child: 3 years, unilateral AOM, fever 38.8°C, bulging TM, daycare attendance (risk of resistant organisms). First-line: Amoxicillin 80–90 mg/kg/day in 2 divided doses for 10 days (5 days for >2 years with mild-moderate symptoms in some guidelines). High-dose amoxicillin covers penicillin-resistant S. pneumoniae. Option A (watchful waiting): Appropriate for children ≥2 years with non-severe, unilateral AOM and reliable follow-up. However, with fever, bulging TM, and daycare (risk of resistant organisms), antibiotic treatment is more appropriate. Option C (amoxicillin-clavulanate): Used if amoxicillin fails (persistent symptoms >48–72 hours), for beta-lactamase producing H. influenzae or M. catarrhalis. Not first-line. Option D (myringotomy): Only for AOM with severe pain, persistent fever despite 48–72 hours antibiotics, or complications. Not immediate first step. High-yield pearl: Most common causative organisms of AOM: S. pneumoniae (most common), H. influenzae (non-typeable), M. catarrhalis. Most spontaneously resolve. Amoxicillin is first-line for non-penicillin-allergic patients. Exam trap: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is NOT first-line — it is for antibiotic failure or confirmed beta-lactamase producers.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 6-year-old child presents with 5 days of right ear pain and fever, not improving on oral antibiotics for AOM. On examination, there is right post-auricular swelling, tenderness, and erythema. The right pinna is displaced anteroinferiorly. CT temporal bone shows opacification of right mastoid air cells with cortical breakdown (mastoid cortex erosion) and a subperiosteal abscess. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: Continue oral antibiotics and add topical drops; review in 5 days
options.B: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics (e.g., ceftriaxone + metronidazole) and cortical mastoidectomy
options.C: IV antibiotics alone for 48 hours and reassess
options.D: Needle aspiration of the subperiosteal abscess in the outpatient clinic

questions.explanation: This is Acute Mastoiditis with Subperiosteal Abscess — a complication of AOM. Features: Post-auricular swelling + tenderness + pinna displaced anteroinferiorly (classic sign), failed oral antibiotic treatment, CT showing cortical breakdown + subperiosteal abscess = surgical indication. Management: (1) IV broad-spectrum antibiotics covering pneumococcus, Staphylococcus, Haemophilus (e.g., IV ceftriaxone ± metronidazole). (2) Cortical mastoidectomy (Schwartze procedure) — surgical drainage of the mastoid air cells and evacuation of the subperiosteal abscess. Cortical mastoidectomy clears mastoid disease while preserving the posterior canal wall and middle ear structures. Option A: Oral antibiotics have failed — this patient now has cortical breakdown and abscess formation; continuing oral antibiotics is inadequate and dangerous (risk of intracranial spread: meningitis, brain abscess, sigmoid sinus thrombosis). Option C: IV antibiotics alone may work for early mastoiditis without abscess or cortical erosion. However, with confirmed cortical breakdown + subperiosteal abscess on CT, surgery is mandatory. Option D: Needle aspiration is inadequate for mastoid abscess (deep disease requiring cortical mastoidectomy). High-yield pearl: Acute coalescent mastoiditis = breakdown of bony septae between mastoid air cells on CT. Complications of mastoiditis: Subperiosteal abscess (most common) → Bezold's abscess (tracking under SCM) → intracranial (meningitis, sigmoid sinus thrombosis, brain abscess, subdural empyema) → Gradenigo's syndrome (petrous apex: V + VI nerve palsy + ear discharge). Exam trap: Pinna displacement: Anteroinferiorly in mastoiditis (post-auricular abscess), Superiorly in parotitis.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old man develops sudden-onset complete right facial palsy (House-Brackmann VI) with severe right ear pain, vesicular eruptions on the right pinna and external auditory canal, and right-sided hearing loss and vertigo. He is diabetic. What is the MOST appropriate treatment?

options.A: Oral prednisolone only, 60 mg/day for 10 days
options.B: IV acyclovir alone for 7 days
options.C: Combined oral valacyclovir + oral prednisolone
options.D: Surgical facial nerve decompression immediately

questions.explanation: This is Ramsay Hunt Syndrome (Herpes Zoster Oticus): Varicella zoster virus reactivation in the geniculate ganglion of the facial nerve. Classic triad: (1) Facial nerve palsy (may be complete HB VI), (2) Otalgia (severe ear pain), (3) Vesicular eruptions in the auricle / EAC / soft palate (Ramsay Hunt zones). Additional features: Sensorineural hearing loss + vertigo (cochlear and vestibular involvement). Diabetes increases risk of severe neuropathy and poorer prognosis. Treatment: Combined antiviral (valacyclovir 1000 mg TID × 7 days OR acyclovir 800 mg 5× daily × 7 days) + corticosteroids (prednisolone 60 mg × 7 days with taper). Combination therapy has better outcomes than either drug alone. Rationale: Antiviral reduces viral replication; corticosteroid reduces nerve oedema and inflammation. Option A (prednisolone only): Inadequate — antiviral therapy is essential for Ramsay Hunt to reduce viral load and nerve damage. Option B (IV acyclovir alone): Antiviral without steroid has poorer outcomes. IV route needed only for immunocompromised or severe disseminated disease. Oral valacyclovir achieves comparable blood levels. Option D (surgical decompression): Reserved for cases with complete palsy showing no improvement at 3 months on electrodiagnostic testing (ENoG <10% on affected side). Not first-line. High-yield pearl: Prognosis: Bell's palsy recovery >95%. Ramsay Hunt recovery: 50–70% (worse with complete palsy and elderly/diabetic). Ramsay Hunt has WORSE prognosis than Bell's palsy due to viral ganglionitis. Exam trap: Ramsay Hunt = VZV, NOT HSV. Bell's palsy = probably HSV-1 reactivation in geniculate ganglion (no vesicles). Treatment: Bell's palsy = prednisolone alone. Ramsay Hunt = prednisolone + antiviral.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 35-year-old factory worker who has worked in a noisy environment for 10 years without ear protection undergoes routine audiometry. He complains of difficulty hearing speech in noisy environments and bilateral tinnitus. Pure tone audiometry shows bilateral symmetrical hearing loss with a characteristic dip at a specific frequency. Which frequency shows the EARLIEST and MOST prominent dip in noise-induced hearing loss?

options.A: 250 Hz

questions.explanation: Noise-induced hearing loss (NIHL) characteristically produces a notch at 4000 Hz (C5 dip / 4-kHz notch). This is the EARLIEST and MOST prominent frequency affected in NIHL. Why 4000 Hz? The area of maximal damage corresponds to a point 8–9 mm from the oval window (basilar membrane tonotopy). The resonant frequency of the ear canal is ~3000 Hz, concentrating energy at 4000 Hz. The blood supply to this region (terminal branches) is more vulnerable to noise trauma. With continued exposure: The notch deepens and broadens to adjacent frequencies (3000 Hz, 6000 Hz, then 2000 Hz). At 8000 Hz (Option D): Also affected but the notch classically begins at 4000 Hz first, recovering slightly at higher frequencies (characteristic V-shaped notch with partial recovery at 8000 Hz). Option A (250 Hz): Low-frequency hearing is preserved longest in NIHL. Option B (1000 Hz): Middle frequency; speech range; affected later. High-yield pearl: C5 dip = 4000 Hz notch = pathognomonic of NIHL. Compare to presbycusis: Gradual bilateral high-frequency sloping loss (no specific notch). Management: NIHL is permanent and irreversible — hearing protection (prevention) is key. Tinnitus is an early symptom. Exam trap: 4000 Hz notch with recovery at 8000 Hz = NIHL. This distinguishes it from presbycusis (sloping loss without recovery) and otosclerosis (Carhart's notch at 2000 Hz).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 40-year-old Chinese man presents with a 3-month history of right-sided nasal obstruction, unilateral blood-stained nasal discharge, right-sided conductive hearing loss, and a painless right neck mass (Level II, 3 cm). He has no history of smoking. Nasendoscopy reveals a ulcero-proliferative mass at the fossa of Rosenmuller (pharyngeal recess). EBV VCA-IgA titres are elevated. MRI of the skull base shows extension to the right cavernous sinus involving cranial nerves V and VI. Biopsy shows WHO Type III (undifferentiated) nasopharyngeal carcinoma. What is the MOST appropriate treatment?

options.A: Total nasopharyngectomy followed by radiotherapy
options.B: Concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiation (chemo + IMRT) to the nasopharynx and neck
options.C: Induction chemotherapy followed by surgery for the neck mass
options.D: Radiotherapy alone to the nasopharynx

questions.explanation: Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma (NPC) staging: This patient has T4 (cavernous sinus/skull base extension, CN V+VI involvement), N1 (ipsilateral single node ≤6 cm), = Stage IVA. Treatment: Concurrent chemoradiation (CRT) = cisplatin-based chemotherapy + Intensity Modulated Radiotherapy (IMRT) is the STANDARD OF CARE for locoregionally advanced NPC (Stage II–IVB). IMRT is preferred over conventional radiotherapy as it spares surrounding critical structures (parotid glands — reduces xerostomia, spinal cord, brainstem). Cisplatin weekly or 3-weekly during radiation acts as radiosensitiser. For Stage III/IV: Induction chemotherapy (TPF or GP regimen) may precede CRT for high tumour burden, but concurrent CRT is the backbone. Option A (surgery): NPC is NOT treated surgically as primary therapy. The nasopharynx is surrounded by critical structures; surgery has unacceptable morbidity. Surgery is reserved for salvage of localised recurrence only. Option C: Induction chemo alone followed by surgery is incorrect — this is a radiosensitive tumour primarily treated with radiation +/- chemo. Option D (RT alone): Only for Stage I (T1N0M0) NPC; all other stages require concurrent chemoradiation (addition of cisplatin improves survival by 20%). High-yield pearl: NPC unique features: Most common primary in fossa of Rosenmuller (lateral nasopharynx). EBV-associated (all WHO types, especially Type II/III). WHO Type III = undifferentiated = most EBV-associated, most radiosensitive. Triad: Posterior nasal obstruction + unilateral secretory otitis media (Eustachian tube obstruction) + neck mass = NPC until proven otherwise. Exam trap: NPC is radiosensitive — surgery is NOT primary treatment. This distinguishes it from most other head and neck cancers.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman with a history of recurrent ear infections in childhood presents with progressive left-sided hearing loss. Otoscopy shows chalky white plaques on the tympanic membrane and in the middle ear. Audiometry shows left-sided conductive hearing loss of 45 dB. Tympanometry shows a Type As (low compliance) curve. What is the pathophysiology of the chalky white plaques seen on the tympanic membrane?

options.A: Calcium pyrophosphate crystal deposition in the middle ear
options.B: Dystrophic calcification of hyalinised collagen in the fibrous layer of the TM
options.C: Cholesterol granuloma formation following haemotympanum
options.D: Keratin debris accumulation from squamous metaplasia

questions.explanation: Tympanosclerosis is the condition characterised by chalky white plaques on the tympanic membrane and/or middle ear structures. Pathophysiology: Repeated episodes of otitis media cause inflammation → hyalinisation of the fibrous (middle) layer of the TM → calcium and phosphate salts are deposited in this hyalinised collagen → dystrophic calcification. These plaques appear white/chalky on otoscopy. In the middle ear: Tympanosclerotic plaques can encase the ossicular chain (especially the incudostapedial joint and stapes footplate) → causing conductive hearing loss. Type As tympanogram = shallow (low compliance) = reduced TM mobility due to plaques or ossicular fixation. Option A: Calcium pyrophosphate deposition = pseudogout, affects large joints, NOT the TM. Option C: Cholesterol granuloma (blue-domed cyst of middle ear) = accumulation of cholesterol crystals after haemotympanum; TM appears bluish, not white. Option D: Keratin debris from squamous metaplasia = cholesteatoma, which appears as white pearly debris in a retraction pocket, not diffuse chalky plaques on TM surface. High-yield pearl: Tympanosclerosis vs Cholesteatoma: Tympanosclerosis = white chalky plaques on TM (dystrophic calcification), conductive HL, NOT associated with foul discharge or bone erosion. Cholesteatoma = white pearly keratin in retraction pocket, foul discharge, bone erosion. Type As tympanogram = also seen in otosclerosis (differentiate by site: otosclerosis = stapes footplate; tympanosclerosis = ossicular chain or TM). Exam trap: Do not confuse tympanosclerosis (chalky plaques = benign) with cholesteatoma (pearly mass in retraction pocket = destructive).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 10-year-old child presents with fever, right-sided periorbital swelling, erythema, proptosis, and painful restriction of extraocular movements in all directions. Visual acuity is reduced to counting fingers in the right eye. CT orbit with contrast shows a rim-enhancing subperiosteal abscess between the lamina papyracea and the medial rectus muscle, with right ethmoid sinusitis. The intraocular pressure is 28 mmHg on the right. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: IV broad-spectrum antibiotics and repeat CT in 24 hours
options.B: Urgent ophthalmology review, IV antibiotics, and lateral canthotomy alone
options.C: Emergency surgical drainage (endoscopic medial orbital decompression + sinus drainage) with IV antibiotics
options.D: Oral antibiotics and nasal decongestants as outpatient and review in 48 hours

questions.explanation: This child has Stage IV orbital complication of sinusitis (Chandler classification) — Subperiosteal Abscess with ophthalmic signs: Proptosis, restricted extraocular movement, reduced visual acuity (counting fingers), elevated IOP (28 mmHg). Chandler Classification of orbital complications: Stage I — Inflammatory oedema (preseptal) Stage II — Orbital cellulitis (postseptal, no abscess) Stage III — Subperiosteal abscess Stage IV — Orbital abscess Stage V — Cavernous sinus thrombosis This is Stage III–IV with visual compromise = SURGICAL EMERGENCY. The combination of subperiosteal abscess + reduced visual acuity + elevated IOP = imminent risk of central retinal artery occlusion and permanent blindness. Management: Emergency endoscopic medial orbital decompression (drain abscess between lamina papyracea and medial rectus) + ethmoidectomy + IV antibiotics (covering S. aureus, S. pneumoniae, anaerobes). Option A: IV antibiotics + watchful waiting is appropriate ONLY for Stage I (preseptal cellulitis) or early Stage II without visual compromise. With confirmed subperiosteal abscess + visual loss, surgical drainage cannot be delayed. Option B: Lateral canthotomy (cantholysis) is used for orbital compartment syndrome to urgently lower IOP, but does not drain a medial subperiosteal abscess — both surgery and ophthalmology input are needed. Option D: Oral antibiotics are completely inadequate for a child with subperiosteal abscess and visual compromise. High-yield pearl: Visual compromise in orbital complications of sinusitis = SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Never delay surgery when: VA reduced, afferent pupillary defect present, IOP elevated. Most common source = ethmoid sinusitis (lamina papyracea is thin, adjacent to orbit). Exam trap: Stage I (preseptal) = IV antibiotics only. Stage III-IV with vision loss = emergency surgical drainage.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child presents with high fever, neck stiffness, difficulty swallowing, and stridor. He had a pharyngitis 5 days ago. He holds his head in extension (opisthotonus-like posture). Lateral neck X-ray shows widening of the prevertebral soft tissue shadow (>7 mm at C2 level). CT neck with contrast confirms a retropharyngeal abscess with rim-enhancement and early mediastinal extension. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: IV amoxicillin-clavulanate and dexamethasone and reassess in 24 hours
options.B: Secure airway first, then transoral drainage of the retropharyngeal abscess
options.C: Transcervical open drainage with midline neck incision
options.D: Flexible nasendoscopy and pus aspiration under sedation in ED

questions.explanation: Retropharyngeal abscess (RPA) in a child <5 years: Retropharyngeal lymph nodes drain the nasopharynx and posterior nasal cavity; they are present in childhood and atrophy by age 5. Upper respiratory infection → retropharyngeal lymphadenitis → suppuration → abscess.
