Hallmarks: Fever, drooling/dysphagia, neck hyperextension (child extends neck to open the airway), muffled voice, stridor (anterior displacement of posterior pharyngeal wall compressing airway), lateral neck X-ray — prevertebral widening >7 mm at C2 or >21 mm at C6 (or >50% of adjacent vertebral body width). Risk of mediastinal extension (descending necrotising mediastinitis) via danger space. MOST CRITICAL: Airway management FIRST — then transoral drainage. Transoral incision and drainage (via the posterior pharyngeal wall under GA) is the standard approach for a localised RPA in a child. Option A: IV antibiotics are essential but an established abscess with mediastinal extension cannot be treated with antibiotics alone. Option C: Transcervical approach is used for parapharyngeal abscess or when transoral approach is not feasible (extensive or inferior extension to mediastinum). For a standard RPA in a child, transoral drainage is preferred as it gives direct access. Option D: Blind aspiration in ED without airway control is dangerous — any sudden rupture can cause aspiration of pus, laryngospasm, and death. High-yield pearl: RPA = most common deep neck space infection in children <5 years. Complication: Descending necrotising mediastinitis (highest mortality). The 'danger space' (between alar and prevertebral fascia) extends from skull base to diaphragm — providing route for mediastinal spread. Exam trap: X-ray threshold for prevertebral soft tissue: >7 mm at C2–C4, >22 mm at C5–C7 suggests retropharyngeal pathology. Always take the X-ray in extension during inspiration for accuracy.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 34-year-old female school teacher presents with persistent hoarseness for 4 months. She uses her voice extensively at work. She denies smoking, alcohol use, or dysphagia. Laryngoscopy reveals bilateral sessile, smooth, symmetrical white/grey lesions at the junction of the anterior and middle thirds of both vocal cords, at the point of maximal vibration. Stroboscopy shows reduced mucosal wave amplitude. What are these lesions?

options.A: Vocal cord polyps — unilateral, pedunculated, haemorrhagic
options.B: Vocal cord nodules (Singer's/Teacher's nodules)
options.C: Reinke's oedema — diffuse bilateral oedematous swelling
options.D: Laryngeal leukoplakia — premalignant lesion requiring biopsy

questions.explanation: This is a classic description of Vocal Cord Nodules (Singer's nodules / Teacher's nodules / Screamer's nodules): Bilateral, symmetrical, at the junction of anterior 1/3 and middle 1/3 (point of maximum vibration during phonation), smooth, sessile, grey/white lesions. Occur in vocal professionals (singers, teachers, preachers) due to phonotrauma — repeated vocal fold collision at maximal vibration point. Stroboscopy confirms reduced mucosal wave (abnormal vibration). Management: Voice therapy (primary and often curative) → if failed: Microsurgical excision (cold steel or microflap technique). Option A (vocal cord polyp): Typically unilateral, pedunculated, haemorrhagic (associated with single vocal trauma/shouting episode or smoking). Option C (Reinke's oedema): Diffuse, bilateral, sausage-like swelling of the entire membranous vocal cord (due to smoking + voice abuse); causes a deep, gravelly voice; associated with hypothyroidism. Option D (leukoplakia): White patch that does NOT wipe off; associated with smoking/GERD; premalignant; requires microlaryngoscopy and biopsy to exclude dysplasia/in situ carcinoma. High-yield pearl: Location of VCN at junction of anterior 1/3 and posterior 2/3 (or anterior 1/3 and middle 1/3) is the HALLMARK — this is where maximum vocal cord collision occurs. All four conditions cause hoarseness but have distinct characteristics: Nodules = bilateral, symmetric, smooth. Polyp = unilateral, pedunculated, haemorrhagic. Reinke's = bilateral, diffuse, smoking-related. Leukoplakia = white patch, unilateral, cannot wipe off. Exam trap: Bilateral symmetrical lesions at this specific location in a voice professional = nodules, NOT polyps or leukoplakia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 2-year-old child with congenital bilateral profound SNHL (confirmed by ABR and ASSR) has failed to show adequate speech development despite 6 months of optimal hearing aid use. HRCT and MRI of the temporal bones show normally developed cochleae bilaterally without inner ear malformations. CT shows patent cochlear turns. What is the MOST appropriate next step?

options.A: Extend hearing aid trial to 2 more years before considering cochlear implant
options.B: Bilateral simultaneous cochlear implantation
options.C: Sign language education as sole rehabilitation
options.D: Auditory brainstem implant (ABI)

questions.explanation: This child has bilateral profound SNHL with failed hearing aid trial (6 months) and no progress in speech and language development. Cochlear implant criteria (paediatric): Age: ≥12 months (FDA approval; earlier in some centres for profoundly deaf). Bilateral profound SNHL (>90 dB PTA). Failed adequate hearing aid trial (3–6 months). No contraindications (cochlear aplasia, auditory nerve aplasia). This child: 2 years, profound bilateral SNHL, failed HA trial, normal cochlear anatomy on CT/MRI = Bilateral simultaneous cochlear implantation. Bilateral cochlear implants: Provide binaural hearing (better localisation, better speech in noise). Simultaneous = both ears in one operation = less risk of second anaesthesia, ensures bilateral fitting before the critical window for auditory cortex development (plasticity period). Option A: Extending hearing aid trial further is inappropriate with confirmed profound SNHL and lack of speech progress — it delays implantation past the critical language development window (age <5 years especially critical). Option C: Sign language alone as sole rehabilitation is NOT recommended as it precludes oral communication; used as supplement, not replacement. Option D (ABI): Used for children with cochlear nerve aplasia or cochlear ossification/aplasia where cochlear implant is not possible. Normal cochlear anatomy here = cochlear implant preferred. High-yield pearl: Earlier cochlear implantation = better speech outcomes (takes advantage of auditory cortical plasticity). Optimal age: 12–18 months for children with congenital deafness. Critical period: Up to 5 years. After age 5, language outcomes decline significantly. Exam trap: Normal cochlear anatomy = cochlear implant. Absent/hypoplastic cochlear nerve = ABI.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 12-year-old boy is brought after a blow to the nose during a football match. He has bilateral nasal obstruction and pain. Examination of the nasal septum with a headlight reveals a smooth, bluish-red, fluctuant bilateral swelling obliterating both nasal cavities. The swelling transilluminates poorly. What is the immediate priority in managing this patient?

options.A: Nasal X-ray to confirm septal fracture
options.B: Oral antibiotics and ice packs for 48 hours
options.C: Immediate incision and drainage with bilateral nasal packing
options.D: CT nose and paranasal sinuses to delineate the haematoma

questions.explanation: This is a septal haematoma — blood accumulates between the perichondrium and septal cartilage after nasal trauma, stripping perichondrium from cartilage and depriving it of blood supply. Signs: Bilateral fluctuant bluish-red swelling of nasal septum, bilateral obstruction (haematoma is between the two layers and expands both sides). It is a clinical EMERGENCY because: Septal cartilage has NO blood vessels — it depends entirely on perichondrium for oxygen/nutrition. If haematoma is not drained urgently → Avascular necrosis of cartilage → Saddle nose deformity (loss of dorsal support). Additionally, the collected blood is an excellent culture medium → risk of septal abscess (usually Staph aureus) → rapid cartilage destruction. Management: Immediate incision and drainage (I&D) under local or general anaesthesia, followed by bilateral nasal packing (to prevent re-accumulation) and systemic antibiotics. Option A: X-ray confirms fracture but diagnosis of haematoma is clinical and does not require imaging. Imaging must not delay drainage. Option B: Antibiotics and ice packs are completely inadequate — the haematoma must be drained. Option D: CT is not needed for clinical diagnosis of septal haematoma and delays treatment. High-yield pearl: Septal haematoma is the #1 emergency of nasal trauma. Remember: Perichondrium = blood supply to cartilage. Haematoma strips perichondrium → ischaemia → necrosis → saddle nose. Septal haematoma → if untreated → septal abscess → even more rapid cartilage destruction. Exam trap: Saddle nose after nasal trauma = missed/untreated septal haematoma in the past. Immediate I&D prevents this.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 4-year-old child presents with progressive hoarseness since age 2 and now has biphasic stridor and episodes of respiratory distress. Flexible laryngoscopy reveals multiple exophytic warty lesions on both vocal cords and the epiglottis. Biopsy confirms recurrent respiratory papillomatosis (RRP). The child has required 8 surgical debridements in the past 2 years. His mother had a history of condyloma acuminata during delivery. Which HPV types are MOST commonly responsible for this condition?

options.A: HPV types 16 and 18
options.B: HPV types 6 and 11
options.C: HPV types 31 and 33
options.D: HPV types 45 and 52

questions.explanation: Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis (RRP) is caused by HPV types 6 and 11 — the same low-risk HPV types that cause condyloma acuminata (genital warts). Type 6: Less aggressive, lower rate of spread. Type 11: More aggressive, higher recurrence rate, risk of pulmonary/tracheal spread, higher risk of malignant transformation. Transmission: Vertical transmission during vaginal delivery from a mother with condyloma acuminata (as in this case). Rarely from infected genital secretions. Juvenile-onset RRP: More aggressive than adult-onset. Most common sites: Vocal cords, then epiglottis, then subglottis. Option A (HPV 16, 18): HIGH-RISK HPV types — cause cervical cancer, oropharyngeal SCC, anal cancer. NOT associated with RRP. Option C (HPV 31, 33): Intermediate/high-risk types — cervical cancer. Not RRP. Option D (HPV 45, 52): High-risk types — cervical cancer. Not RRP. Treatment: Serial surgical microlaryngoscopy with CO2 laser or cold steel debulking (debridement — cannot cure, only debulk). Adjuvant therapy for aggressive disease: Bevacizumab (anti-VEGF) or intralesional cidofovir. Prevention: HPV quadrivalent vaccine (types 6, 11, 16, 18) reduces maternal genital wart infection → reduces vertical transmission. High-yield pearl: RRP = most common benign laryngeal tumour in children. HPV 6 and 11 = low-risk types = RRP and condyloma. HPV 16 and 18 = high-risk types = cancers. Exam trap: Don't confuse HPV typing: 6 and 11 = low-risk = papilloma/warts. 16 and 18 = high-risk = carcinoma.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 6-month-old infant is referred for hearing assessment after failing the newborn hearing screen twice. He was born prematurely at 30 weeks, required NICU care, and received gentamicin. What is the MOST appropriate investigation to confirm hearing thresholds in this infant?

options.A: Pure tone audiometry (PTA)
options.B: Auditory Brainstem Response (ABR/BAEP) with frequency-specific stimuli
options.C: Distortion Product Otoacoustic Emissions (DPOAEs)
options.D: Behavioural observation audiometry (BOA)

questions.explanation: For diagnostic hearing threshold estimation in a 6-month-old infant: Frequency-specific (tone-burst) ABR (Auditory Brainstem Response) is the gold standard. Why ABR? Objective, no behavioural response required (does not require active cooperation), measures neural pathway from cochlea to brainstem, provides ear-specific and frequency-specific threshold estimation, valid at any age including neonates. ABR components: Wave I = cochlear nerve. Wave II = cochlear nucleus. Wave III = superior olivary complex. Wave IV = lateral lemniscus. Wave V = inferior colliculus. In aminoglycoside (gentamicin) ototoxicity and prematurity — risk of cochlear SNHL — ABR accurately identifies the degree and configuration of loss. Option A (PTA): Requires voluntary response (pressing a button when hearing a tone); valid in cooperative children ≥5 years only. Not applicable at 6 months. Option C (DPOAEs): Tests outer hair cell function; used as SCREENING tool (present/absent). Does NOT provide frequency-specific thresholds. A pass on DPOAE does not rule out auditory neuropathy or retrocochlear pathology. Option D (BOA): Behavioural observation (observing reflex responses to sound) is unreliable and not used for diagnostic threshold estimation in infants <6 months. High-yield pearl: Newborn hearing screen tests: TEOAE (Transient Evoked OAE) or ABR (automated ABR = AABR). If screen fails: Diagnostic ABR (frequency-specific) = gold standard to confirm thresholds. Exam trap: DPOAE/TEOAE pass does NOT rule out ALL hearing loss — it only tests outer hair cells. Auditory neuropathy spectrum disorder (ANSD) = normal OAEs + absent ABR. In NICU babies (risk for ANSD from gentamicin, hyperbilirubinemia, asphyxia): Use AABR for screening, not OAE alone.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 25-year-old man presents with a painless, smooth, fluctuant swelling in the left anterior triangle of the neck, anterior to the upper third of the sternocleidomastoid muscle. It appeared 3 weeks ago after an upper respiratory tract infection. FNAC shows cholesterol crystals with lymphocytes and squamous cells. What is the MOST likely diagnosis and its appropriate treatment?

options.A: Thyroglossal cyst — moves with swallowing and tongue protrusion; treatment is Sistrunk's operation
options.B: Branchial cyst (2nd branchial arch remnant) — excision after infection has resolved
options.C: Cystic hygroma (lymphatic malformation) — sclerotherapy with OK-432
options.D: Dermoid cyst — excision with primary closure

questions.explanation: Classic presentation of a branchial (cleft) cyst: Young adult, anterior triangle of neck, anterior to upper 1/3 of SCM (Level II), fluctuant, often presents/enlarges after URTI (when lymphoid tissue in the cyst wall swells). FNAC: Cholesterol crystals + lymphocytes + squamous cells = diagnostic of branchial cyst. Pathology: 2nd branchial arch/cleft remnant lined by squamous epithelium with lymphoid tissue in wall. Embryology: Second branchial arch overgrowth fails to cover 2nd–4th cleft → cervical sinus of His → branchial cyst, sinus, or fistula. Treatment: Excision (complete, including the tract if sinus/fistula present) — performed after acute infection resolves. Never drain acutely (risks fistula formation and incomplete excision). Important: In patients >40 years: A cystic neck mass in Level II should be considered a cystic metastasis from SCC (tonsillar or HPV-related) until proven otherwise — requires urgent panendoscopy, not just excision. Option A (thyroglossal cyst): Midline, moves with tongue protrusion and swallowing, associated with thyroid tissue, located near hyoid bone. Sistrunk's operation = excision of cyst + central hyoid + tract to foramen caecum. Option C (cystic hygroma): Transilluminates brilliantly, multiloculated, found in posterior triangle, presents in infancy/childhood (not young adults). Option D (dermoid cyst): Usually midline (floor of mouth, submental), contains hair/sebum, does not contain cholesterol crystals. High-yield pearl: Branchial cyst FNAC = cholesterol crystals + lymphocytes + squamous epithelium. In a patient >40 years with a 'branchial cyst': High suspicion for cystic metastasis from occult SCC (oropharyngeal HPV cancer) — full workup before excision. Exam trap: Branchial cyst is Level II (upper anterior triangle, SCM). Thyroglossal cyst is midline. Never aspirate/incise an infected branchial cyst acutely.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man with T4a laryngeal cancer requires total laryngectomy. He is currently intubated in ICU following aspiration pneumonia. The team plans a tracheostomy to wean him from ventilator prior to definitive surgery. A surgical tracheostomy is performed. On post-operative day 2, the tracheostomy tube becomes accidentally dislodged and cannot be easily reinserted. There is respiratory distress. What is the MOST appropriate immediate action?

options.A: Attempt blind reinsertion of the tracheostomy tube through the stoma
options.B: Oral endotracheal intubation as a temporising measure
options.C: Oxygenate via bag-mask ventilation through the stoma and call for senior help
options.D: Insert an appropriately sized tracheal dilator/airway device through the stoma with direct vision and maintain oxygenation

questions.explanation: Accidental decannulation within the first 72–96 hours of surgical tracheostomy = CRITICAL EMERGENCY. During this period, the tracheostomy tract has NOT matured (no epithelialised tract formed yet). If tube is dislodged: The stoma can rapidly close/collapse. Blind reinsertion attempts can create a FALSE PASSAGE — tube goes into subcutaneous tissue or anterior mediastinum, not trachea → worsening hypoxia, surgical emphysema, death. Management (as per UK National Tracheostomy Safety Project guidelines): 1. Call for help immediately. 2. Provide oxygen at the stoma (via face mask or bag-valve-mask placed over the stoma). 3. Attempt to insert a TRACHEAL DILATOR (bougie/tracheal dilator/suction catheter) under direct vision to maintain stoma patency → then railroad the tracheostomy tube over the dilator. 4. If stoma collapses and cannot be visualised: Oral intubation is the bailout (the larynx is still patent, as this is NOT a laryngectomy patient). Key distinction: If this were post-total laryngectomy: Oral intubation is IMPOSSIBLE (larynx has been removed). Stoma ventilation only. Option A (blind reinsertion): Never blind — risk of false passage. Option B (orotracheal intubation): This patient has an intact larynx (tracheostomy, not laryngectomy) → oral intubation is a valid backup if stoma approach fails. But it should NOT be the FIRST step — you must first attempt to maintain/reinsert via the stoma with a dilator. Option C (BVM through stoma alone): Can provide temporary oxygenation but BVM is a poor seal on a stoma — definitive reinsertion is needed. High-yield pearl: Tracheostomy emergencies: <7 days post-op = no mature tract → use dilator + reinsertion. >7 days = mature tract → may reinsert tube directly. Post-laryngectomy decannulation = stoma ONLY. Cannot intubate orally. Exam trap: Post-laryngectomy patient = oral intubation is impossible (no larynx). Post-tracheostomy patient = oral intubation is possible as backup.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 14-year-old boy presents with severe headache, fever (39.5°C), nausea, and vomiting for 3 days. He has a 2-week history of left ear pain and discharge. Examination reveals a bulging left tympanic membrane with purulent discharge. He has neck stiffness and photophobia. Fundoscopy shows bilateral papilloedema. CT head shows no intracranial mass, but a defect in the left tegmen tympani with left temporal lobe hypodensity and rim-enhancing lesion. CSF analysis: WBC 1800 cells/µL (polymorphonuclear), protein 220 mg/dL, glucose 18 mg/dL (serum glucose 90 mg/dL). Blood cultures pending. What is the MOST appropriate management?

options.A: IV dexamethasone + IV ceftriaxone + lumbar puncture for culture, then treat the ear
options.B: Emergency mastoidectomy to drain the ear, antibiotics, and neurosurgical consultation for the brain abscess
options.C: Immediate neurosurgical craniotomy for brain abscess evacuation, followed by ear surgery later
options.D: IV vancomycin + meropenem + antifungal and monitor conservatively

questions.explanation: This is a catastrophic intracranial complication of acute otitis media: Brain Abscess (temporal lobe) + Meningitis. Evidence: AOM (left ear discharge, bulging TM) → tegmen tympani defect (bone erosion above middle ear → intracranial spread) → left temporal lobe ring-enhancing lesion (brain abscess) + CSF pleocytosis/meningitis picture + papilloedema (raised ICP). Management of brain abscess complicating AOM requires SIMULTANEOUS ENT + Neurosurgical management: (1) ENT: Emergency mastoidectomy — eradicates the source (infected middle ear/mastoid) and drains middle ear. Without this, the brain abscess will recur. (2) Neurosurgery: Stereotactic aspiration or craniotomy evacuation of the temporal lobe abscess (depending on size and neurological status). (3) IV antibiotics: Covering gram-positive cocci, gram-negatives, anaerobes — typically ceftriaxone + metronidazole ± vancomycin. Option A: Treating meningitis with antibiotics alone without addressing the source (ear) is inadequate — brain abscess requires surgical drainage; lumbar puncture with papilloedema and mass lesion is CONTRAINDICATED (risk of tentorial herniation). Option C: Neurosurgical craniotomy without mastoidectomy = treating the consequence without the source → high recurrence risk. Option D: Conservative IV antibiotics alone for a temporal lobe brain abscess > 2 cm = inappropriate; surgical drainage needed. High-yield pearl: Intracranial complications of otitis media: Meningitis (most common), Brain abscess (temporal lobe from middle ear, cerebellar from mastoid), Sigmoid sinus thrombosis (Quinlan's triad: fever, neck rigidity, temporal headache), Subdural empyema, Extradural abscess, Otitic hydrocephalus (raised ICP without abscess — from sigmoid sinus thrombosis). Exam trap: LP is CONTRAINDICATED when papilloedema or mass lesion is present — herniation risk. Treat with empirical antibiotics + imaging first.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman presents with complete loss of smell (anosmia) following a car accident 6 months ago. She struck her forehead on the dashboard. She has no nasal obstruction, no history of sinusitis, and nasal endoscopy is normal. Olfactory testing (Sniffin' Sticks) confirms anosmia bilaterally. Taste sensation and sense of flavour are also impaired. What is the MOST likely mechanism of her anosmia?

options.A: Obstruction of the olfactory cleft by post-traumatic mucosal oedema
options.B: Shearing of the olfactory fila (filaments) passing through the cribriform plate
options.C: Injury to the olfactory bulb due to direct fracture of the cribriform plate
options.D: Hippocampal damage affecting olfactory memory and recognition

questions.explanation: Post-traumatic anosmia is the most common cause of permanent anosmia in adults. The mechanism: Head trauma (especially frontal/occipital impact) causes rapid acceleration-deceleration → shearing forces sever the delicate olfactory fila (olfactory nerve filaments — the 1st cranial nerve) as they pass through the tiny foramina of the cribriform plate → immediate, complete anosmia. Normal nasal endoscopy (no mucosal disease) and bilateral anosmia = central/nerve cause. This patient has: Forehead impact + bilateral anosmia + normal nasal endoscopy + impaired flavour (retronasal olfaction lost) = post-traumatic anosmia from cribriform plate olfactory fila shearing. Option A (mucosal oedema at olfactory cleft): Causes conductive anosmia — typically resolves. Would be present on nasal endoscopy. Not the mechanism for permanent post-traumatic anosmia. Option C (cribriform plate fracture): Possible in severe trauma; may cause CSF rhinorrhoea. However, the primary mechanism of post-traumatic anosmia is olfactory fila shearing, NOT the fracture itself (fracture per se doesn't damage olfaction — the fila crossing the plate do). Option D (hippocampal damage): Hippocampus is involved in memory encoding but is not the primary olfactory processing centre (that is the olfactory cortex/piriform cortex). Hippocampal damage causes amnesia, not primary anosmia. High-yield pearl: 2 types of anosmia: Conductive (blocked nasal airflow to olfactory cleft — sinusitis, polyps, rhinitis) vs. Sensorineural (damage to olfactory nerve/bulb — post-viral, post-traumatic, Parkinson's, Alzheimer's). Post-COVID anosmia: Injury to sustentacular cells + direct olfactory neuroepithelium damage. Post-traumatic: Olfactory fila shearing. Exam trap: Flavour = taste + retronasal olfaction. If olfaction is lost → both taste and flavour are impaired (patient describes 'loss of taste'). True taste (salt, sweet, bitter, sour, umami) tests via cranial nerves VII and IX — usually normal in post-traumatic anosmia.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man with a 40-pack-year smoking history and chronic alcohol use presents with progressive dysphagia (initially solids, now liquids), 10 kg weight loss, left-sided otalgia (referred pain), and a hard left Level III neck node (4 cm). Flexible laryngoscopy shows a large fungating mass in the left pyriform sinus with pooling of secretions. CT neck/chest shows hypopharyngeal mass with left neck lymphadenopathy (Stage T3 N2b M0). What is the treatment of choice?

options.A: Total pharyngolaryngectomy with reconstruction + postoperative chemoradiation
options.B: Concurrent cisplatin-based chemoradiation with larynx-preservation intent
options.C: Induction chemotherapy (TPF) alone to assess response
options.D: Palliative radiotherapy to neck + systemic chemotherapy

questions.explanation: Hypopharyngeal cancer (pyriform sinus carcinoma) management: This patient has T3 N2b M0 pyriform sinus SCC = Stage IVA (locoregionally advanced but technically resectable). For T3 hypopharyngeal SCC: The VA Larynx Trial and RTOG 91-11 established that larynx preservation with concurrent chemoradiation is an alternative to total laryngopharyngectomy, with equivalent overall survival. Concurrent chemoradiation (cisplatin + IMRT): Offers larynx preservation in ~50–60% of cases, equivalent survival to surgery for selected patients. This is preferable to mutilating surgery as primary approach in patients without cartilage invasion or airway obstruction requiring immediate surgical palliation. Option A (total pharyngolaryngectomy): This is the alternative definitive treatment. It is preferred when: Airway is compromised, Patient cannot tolerate chemoradiation, After failure of larynx-preservation CRT, or Tumour shows thyroid cartilage destruction. With adequate pulmonary function and performance status, larynx-preservation is attempted first. Option C (induction chemo alone): TPF induction followed by CRT is used in selected centres as a larynx-preservation strategy (e.g., TAX 324 trial), but concurrent CRT alone (without induction) is still the standard approach per RTOG guidelines. Option D (palliative): Not appropriate for resectable T3N2bM0 disease with curative intent. High-yield pearl: Pyriform sinus = most common site of hypopharyngeal carcinoma. Silent tumour — presents late with large neck nodes, referred otalgia (via Arnold's nerve/Jacobson's nerve). Referred otalgia from hypopharyngeal/oropharyngeal cancer = ominous sign (deep invasion of vagal/glossopharyngeal branches). Exam trap: Referred otalgia causes: External ear normal → referred via CN V (TM/TJ joint), CN IX (tonsillar/BOT), CN X (hypopharynx/larynx). 'Otalgia with normal ear' = always look for head and neck primary.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman presents with sudden onset severe vertigo, nausea, vomiting, and inability to walk that started 2 days ago. She has no hearing loss or tinnitus. Neurological examination: Normal finger-nose test, no nystagmus on forward gaze, but on testing the HEAD IMPULSE TEST (HIT): Positive right head impulse (corrective saccade seen when head rotated rapidly to the right). Romberg's test shows falling to the right with eyes closed. Skew deviation is absent. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.A: Right posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) infarct
options.B: Right acute vestibular neuritis (vestibular neuronitis)
options.C: Bilateral vestibular failure
options.D: Right Meniere's disease attack

questions.explanation: This is Acute Vestibular Neuritis (AVN) presenting with the classic HINTS bedside examination: H — Head Impulse Test (HIT): Positive right (corrective saccade on right) = peripheral lesion. A positive HIT indicates an ipsilateral peripheral vestibular defect (vestibuloocular reflex failure on the side being tested). I — INFAST (Nystagmus assessment): Not described as direction-changing (would indicate central). N — No Skew deviation. S — No SNHL, no tinnitus. HINTS mnemonic differentiates dangerous (central stroke) from benign (peripheral): Peripheral AVN: Positive HIT (unilateral), Unidirectional horizontal nystagmus (fast phase away from lesion), No skew deviation = SAFE. Central (posterior fossa stroke): Negative HIT (normal), Direction-changing nystagmus, Skew deviation = DANGEROUS. This patient: positive HIT (right) + no skew + falls to right (right vestibular hypofunction) + no hearing loss = Right acute vestibular neuritis. Option A (PICA infarct/Wallenberg syndrome): Would have NEGATIVE HIT (normal), skew deviation, other brainstem signs (dysphagia, ipsilateral Horner's, contralateral pain/temperature loss). Option C (bilateral vestibular failure): Both HIT would be positive; oscillopsia during head movement; rare. Option D (Meniere's): Associated with tinnitus, low-frequency SNHL, and aural fullness — absent here. High-yield pearl: HINTS exam = better than MRI at 48 hours for distinguishing acute peripheral vertigo from central stroke (sensitivity >96% vs MRI ~80% at <48 hrs). Positive HIT = reassuring (peripheral). Skew deviation = alarming (central). Exam trap: Head impulse test: 'Positive' = BAD for the tested side = peripheral defect. 'Negative' (no corrective saccade) + acute severe vertigo = alarming = possible posterior stroke.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man presents with 18-month history of unilateral right nasal obstruction and unilateral blood-stained nasal discharge. Nasal endoscopy reveals a grey, polypoid lesion arising from the right lateral nasal wall at the middle meatus. CT PNS shows a lobulated mass filling the right nasal cavity and right maxillary sinus with a 'convoluted cerebriform' pattern and focal areas of calcification. Biopsy shows an inverted papilloma with hyperplastic respiratory epithelium inverted into the underlying stroma. What is the MOST important concern about this tumour?

options.A: Rapid bilateral spread via the nasal septum requiring bilateral nasal surgery
options.B: Risk of synchronous or metachronous malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma
options.C: High risk of intracranial extension at initial presentation
options.D: Association with EBV requiring antiviral treatment before surgery

questions.explanation: Inverted Papilloma (Schneiderian papilloma, transitional cell papilloma) — Important oncological concern: Malignant transformation to squamous cell carcinoma occurs in approximately 10–15% of cases, either synchronously (SCC present at diagnosis) or metachronously (SCC develops in recurrent papilloma after surgery). This is the MOST important clinical concern because: (1) It mandates adequate surgical excision (not simple polypectomy), (2) It requires long-term endoscopic surveillance post-excision, (3) Any recurrence needs re-biopsy to exclude malignant transformation. Treatment: Endoscopic medial maxillectomy (FESS with complete resection of the tumour base and affected bone) — simple polypectomy has very high recurrence rates (70–80%) due to incomplete removal. Option A (bilateral spread): Inverted papilloma is characteristically UNILATERAL. Bilateral involvement suggests multicentricity or advanced disease but is NOT the most important concern. Option C (intracranial extension): Occurs in advanced (Stage IV) disease — uncommon at initial presentation. Not the most important concern here. Option D (EBV): EBV is NOT associated with inverted papilloma. HPV (types 6, 11, and occasionally 16, 18) have been detected in inverted papilloma but a causative role is not definitively established. High-yield pearl: Inverted papilloma characteristics: Unilateral, lateral nasal wall (middle meatus/turbinate), 'inverted' epithelium grows INTO stroma (opposite of exophytic papilloma), 'convoluted cerebriform' CT pattern = characteristic, High recurrence (30–50%) after incomplete removal, 10–15% risk of SCC transformation. Exam trap: Inverted papilloma = benign tumour but with malignant potential. NEVER treat by simple polypectomy — must resect with adequate margins. Long-term surveillance essential.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 52-year-old man presents with a 4-month history of a rapidly enlarging right parotid mass associated with right-sided facial weakness (House-Brackmann IV). The mass is firm, fixed, and tender. He previously had a pleomorphic adenoma excised from the same gland 15 years ago. CT shows a heterogeneous, ill-defined right parotid mass with skull base extension. FNAC shows malignant epithelial cells with areas of carcinoma and residual benign pleomorphic adenoma features. What is the MOST likely diagnosis?

options.A: Mucoepidermoid carcinoma (high-grade)
options.B: Carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma
options.C: Adenoid cystic carcinoma
options.D: Acinic cell carcinoma

questions.explanation: Carcinoma ex-pleomorphic adenoma (CXPA) — Classic scenario: Previous benign pleomorphic adenoma → malignant transformation after years (typically 10–20 years). Risk: ~1% at 5 years, increasing to ~10% at 15 years — reasons why large/longstanding pleomorphic adenomas must be excised. Hallmarks of CXPA: Prior diagnosis of pleomorphic adenoma, Rapid growth in a previously stable parotid mass, Facial nerve palsy (NEVER occurs in benign parotid tumours — immediate sign of malignancy), Fixation and infiltration, FNAC shows malignant cells + residual benign PA areas. This combination is pathognomonic of CXPA. Option A (mucoepidermoid carcinoma): Most common parotid malignancy overall. Does NOT arise from pre-existing pleomorphic adenoma. Usually no prior benign diagnosis. Option C (adenoid cystic carcinoma): Characterised by perineural invasion (facial numbness/pain), not rapid growth from pre-existing PA. Cribriform pattern on histology ('Swiss cheese'). Option D (acinic cell carcinoma): Low-grade, indolent, does NOT arise from PA. High-yield pearl: Parotid gland malignancy indicators: Facial nerve palsy (HB III or worse), Fixation to skin/deeper structures, Rapid growth, Hard/irregular lump, Cervical lymphadenopathy, Skin involvement. All indicate malignancy until proven otherwise. Malignant transformation from pleomorphic adenoma = Carcinoma ex-PA = rapidly growing mass in previously known PA. Exam trap: 'Painless slow-growing parotid mass with facial nerve intact' = most likely benign. 'Facial nerve palsy + parotid mass' = malignancy (CXPA, high-grade mucoepidermoid, or adenoid cystic carcinoma with perineural invasion).

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 72-year-old poorly controlled diabetic man presents with severe, unrelenting right ear pain (worse at night), purulent otorrhea, and itching for 3 weeks. He has not responded to two courses of topical antibiotic drops. Examination reveals granulation tissue at the bony-cartilaginous junction of the right external auditory canal. Cranial nerve examination shows right facial palsy (House-Brackmann IV). CT temporal bone shows bone erosion at the EAC floor with extension to the stylomastoid foramen. Tc-99m bone scan shows increased uptake at the temporal bone. What is the MOST appropriate treatment?

options.A: Prolonged topical ciprofloxacin ear drops for 6 weeks
options.B: IV anti-pseudomonal antibiotics (e.g., IV ciprofloxacin or ceftazidime) for 6–12 weeks
options.C: Surgical debridement of granulation tissue and oral co-amoxiclav
options.D: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy alone

questions.explanation: Malignant (Necrotising) Otitis Externa (MOE): A severe, potentially life-threatening invasive infection of the external auditory canal and surrounding skull base in elderly diabetics or immunocompromised patients. Pathogen: Pseudomonas aeruginosa (responsible for >95% of cases). Hallmarks: Elderly diabetic, unrelenting severe otalgia (disproportionate to clinical signs), granulation tissue at bony-cartilaginous junction (pathognomonic), skull base osteomyelitis on CT, Tc-99m scan shows uptake (confirms osteomyelitis). Complications: Cranial nerve palsies (order of involvement: VII → IX, X, XI → XII) due to skull base spread. Treatment: Prolonged systemic anti-pseudomonal antibiotics for 6–12 weeks: IV ciprofloxacin (fluoroquinolone, excellent Pseudomonas activity and bone penetration) or IV ceftazidime. Duration: Until bone scan normalises (may take months). Serial Gallium-67 scans to monitor response (Tc-99m shows any osteoblastic activity; Ga-67 is better for monitoring inflammatory response). Option A: Topical drops are inadequate for skull base osteomyelitis — systemic therapy is mandatory. Option C: Surgical debridement has a limited role — used for biopsy to confirm diagnosis and debulk granulation tissue, but does NOT replace antibiotics; extensive surgery is avoided in diabetics (poor healing). Option D: Hyperbaric oxygen is used as ADJUNCT therapy in refractory MOE, not monotherapy. High-yield pearl: MOE = Pseudomonas + Diabetic/immunocompromised + Skull base osteomyelitis = IV ciprofloxacin 6–12 weeks. Facial nerve palsy in MOE indicates spread to stylomastoid foramen (where CN VII exits skull). Order of CN palsy in MOE: VII (most common) → IX, X, XI → XII (hypoglossal, least common). Exam trap: Granulation tissue at bony-cartilaginous junction of EAC = RED FLAG = rule out MOE in elderly diabetics. Regular OE has itching/discharge — MOE has SEVERE UNRELENTING PAIN.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman presents 18 months after rhinoplasty with progressive nasal tip ptosis, loss of tip projection, and worsening nasal obstruction. She is distressed about her appearance. On examination, the nasal tip is drooping and pinched, alar cartilages are over-resected, and there is internal nasal valve collapse on inspiration (Cottle manoeuvre positive). What is the MOST likely cause of her current symptoms?

options.A: Infection of the nasal cartilage causing septic necrosis
options.B: Over-resection of the lower lateral cartilages (alar cartilages) during rhinoplasty
options.C: Septal perforation from aggressive septoplasty during the procedure
options.D: Hypertrophic scarring of the nasal skin causing contracture

questions.explanation: This patient has classic post-rhinoplasty complications from over-resection of the lower lateral (alar) cartilages: (1) Nasal tip ptosis — loss of tip support from alar cartilage struts. (2) Pinched tip — excessive lateral crural resection narrows the nostril aperture. (3) Internal nasal valve collapse — lower lateral cartilages normally support the internal nasal valve (15° angle between septum and upper lateral cartilage); over-resection → valve collapse on inspiration → nasal obstruction. (4) Loss of tip projection — cartilage struts maintain tip projection; loss = ptosis. Cottle manoeuvre: Lateral cheek retraction to open nasal valve — if breathing improves, confirms nasal valve dysfunction. The alar cartilages provide the structural support of the nasal tip and nostrils. Over-aggressive cephalic trim (resection of the cephalic portion of lower lateral cartilage) during rhinoplasty is the most common cause of these problems. Option A (infection/septic necrosis): Would present acutely with pain, erythema, fever, and purulent discharge — not 18 months later with structural collapse. Option C (septal perforation): Presents with whistling, crusting, epistaxis, or midline septal defect — not tip ptosis. Option D (hypertrophic scarring): Nasal skin contracture could affect tip position but is less likely to cause valve collapse. High-yield pearl: Cottle manoeuvre = lateral traction on cheek skin → opens internal nasal valve → improvement in breathing = positive Cottle = internal nasal valve collapse. External nasal valve = nares opening (alar cartilage inferior rim). Internal nasal valve = junction of upper lateral cartilage and septum. Treatment of post-rhinoplasty valve collapse: Spreader grafts (septal cartilage grafts) to widen internal valve. Exam trap: Never over-resect alar cartilages — leave at least 5–7 mm of lateral crus to maintain valve competence and structural support.

questions.subject: ENT
questions.question_text: A neonate is diagnosed with bilateral profound SNHL on newborn hearing screening. The parents are non-consanguineous with no family history of deafness. Ophthalmological examination is normal. The infant has no other congenital anomalies. Genetic testing identifies a homozygous pathogenic variant in the GJB2 gene (c.35delG). What is the MOST appropriate statement regarding this genetic finding?

options.A: GJB2 mutations cause progressive hearing loss associated with retinitis pigmentosa (Usher syndrome)
options.B: GJB2 (connexin 26) mutations are the most common cause of autosomal recessive non-syndromic SNHL
options.C: Mitochondrial DNA mutations are more commonly identified in bilateral profound congenital deafness than GJB2
options.D: GJB2 mutation-associated SNHL is typically unilateral and mild-moderate

questions.explanation: GJB2 gene encodes Connexin 26 (Cx26), a gap junction protein essential for potassium (K+) recycling in the cochlea (from hair cells back to the endolymph via the supporting cells and stria vascularis). Mutations in GJB2 are the MOST COMMON cause of autosomal recessive non-syndromic sensorineural hearing loss (DFNB1 locus): Account for ~50% of cases of autosomal recessive non-syndromic SNHL. c.35delG (35delG) is the MOST COMMON GJB2 pathogenic variant in Caucasian and Mediterranean populations. The hearing loss is: Bilateral, typically severe-profound, Non-progressive (usually congenital), Non-syndromic (no other anomalies). This infant: Normal eyes, no other anomalies, non-consanguineous parents, homozygous 35delG = classic GJB2 non-syndromic SNHL. Option A: Usher syndrome (retinitis pigmentosa + SNHL) is caused by MYO7A, CDH23, PCDH15, and other genes — NOT GJB2. Connexin 26 does NOT cause Usher syndrome. Option C: Mitochondrial mutations (mtDNA, e.g., m.1555A>G causing aminoglycoside sensitivity) are less common causes of SNHL. GJB2 mutations are far more common in bilateral congenital profound SNHL. Option D: GJB2 SNHL is typically BILATERAL and SEVERE-PROFOUND, not unilateral or mild. High-yield pearl: Genetics of SNHL: Most common: GJB2 (Connexin 26) — DFNB1 — autosomal recessive, non-syndromic, bilateral, profound. Syndromic SNHL causes: Waardenburg (PAX3, MITF) = pigmentation abnormalities. Usher (MYO7A) = retinitis pigmentosa. Pendred (SLC26A4) = goitre + SNHL. Jervell-Lange-Nielsen (KCNQ1) = prolonged QT + SNHL. Exam trap: GJB2/Connexin 26 = non-syndromic = no other anomalies. Always check eyes in bilateral profound congenital SNHL (to exclude Usher syndrome = progressive blindness).
